b.bio: Two men named Pietro Paolo Vergerio must be kept apart. The surviving records describe only Vergerio the Younger (born 1497/98 at Capodistria, died October 4, 1565 at Tübingen): a jurist trained at Padua who practiced law, papal nuncio to Germany from 1533, bishop successively of Modruš and Capodistria (1536), who met Luther at Wittenberg while pursuing council business, was accused of Lutheranism, left Italy, corresponded with the Zurich reformers, and ended as a Protestant reformer in Switzerland and Württemberg. None of The surviving records covers Vergerio the Elder, the Capodistrian humanist of the late fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries. The library's single work sits among the Latin Fathers in Migne's Patrologia Latina (vol. 22) alongside Jerome — a placement consistent with an earlier patristic-era or humanist author rather than the sixteenth-century reformer, but no surviving record attributes this prayer to either man, so the dates and identity of the author of the held work are left unstated.
b.s: The work held here is a two-page prayer on Saint Jerome: it praises Jerome as exceeding all human praise, argues that devotion toward God and the saints benefits the one praying rather than God, who needs no worship, that the saints' merits and intercession obtain benefits for the living, and that the righteous dead enjoy nearer access to the saints; it also defends Jerome against his slanderous rivals, citing Gregory Nazianzen.

b.bio: Gregory I was born in Rome around 540, the son of a Roman senator, and served as prefect of the city at about age 30 before living in a monastery he established on his family estate. He acted as a papal ambassador (to Constantinople) and became Bishop of Rome on 3 September 590, holding the see until his death on 12 March 604. As pope he improved the welfare of the people of Rome, combated the Donatist heresy popular in North Africa, regained papal authority in Spain and France, and sent missionaries to England, including Augustine of Canterbury. He wrote more prolifically than any previous pope and was known in the Middle Ages as 'the Father of Christian Worship'. The library also holds several liturgical and exegetical pieces under his name — the Book of Sacraments, Antiphonary, Responsorial Book, and Exposition on the Song of Songs — which circulated under his name in later centuries.
b.s: The works here span his biblical exegesis (Moralia on Job, Homilies on Ezekiel and the Gospels), pastoral governance (Pastoral Rule, Letters), and hagiography (Dialogues), alongside liturgical books; he is regarded as a principal bridge between patristic theology and the medieval church, and a founder of the medieval papacy.

b.bio: The library's two items under this name are a privilege for a monastery and a letter on excommunication; these belong to Adeodatus II, not to Deusdedit (Adeodatus I, pope 615–618). Adeodatus II was a monk of the Roman cloister of St. Erasmus on the Coelian Hill before his election on 11 April 672. He was active in perfecting monastic discipline and in repressing Monothelitism, though he played no known role in its political liquidation. Of his correspondence only the letters for the abbeys of St. Peter of Canterbury and St. Martin of Tours are preserved.
b.s: The works held here are among the few surviving acts of his pontificate: papal privileges securing monastic exemption from episcopal and lay exactions and free abbatial election, grounded in the authority of the apostolic see.

b.bio: Agatho was born in Sicily around 577 and became bishop of Rome on 27 June 678, succeeding Donus. He heard the appeal of Wilfrid of York against his deposition by Theodore of Canterbury and ordered his restoration. His pontificate's chief event was the Sixth Ecumenical Council at Constantinople (680–681), convened against Monothelitism; Agatho sent legates and a letter defining two wills in Christ, which the council accepted. He died in Rome on 10 January 681, before the council's decrees reached him for approval. He is venerated as a saint in both the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches.
b.s: The letters held here include the dogmatic letter to Constantinople that supplied the council's definition of two wills in Christ and helped end the Monothelite controversy.

b.bio:
Pietro Ballerini (1698–1769) — Pietro Ballerini, born at Verona 7 September 1698, died there 28 March 1769, was a secular priest who served as principal of a classical school in Verona. With his brother Girolamo he edited the works of Cardinal Noris (1729–33), the writings of Bishop Matteo Giberti (1733), and a critical edition of the sermons of St. Zeno of Verona (1739). He defended Probabiliorism against the absolute Probabilists, wrote against usury, and edited the summae of St. Antoninus and St. Raymond of Penyafort. At the request of Benedict XIV he produced a complete edition of Leo the Great, refuting Quesnel's defective version. He also wrote on the primacy and infallibility of the Roman pontiffs.

Girolamo Ballerini (1701–1781) — Girolamo Ballerini, born at Verona 29 January 1701 (the New Catholic Dictionary prints 1702), died there 23 April 1781. Educated at the Jesuit college and seminary of Verona, he was ordained a secular priest. With his brother Pietro he published joint works: a complete edition of Cardinal Noris (1729–33), an edition of Matteo Giberti (1733), and a critical edition of the sermons of St. Zeno of Verona (1739). The works held here are his editorial apparatus — prefaces, dissertations, indices, and disquisitions — for Migne's Patrologia volumes on Zeno, Ratherius, Leo the Great, Ivo of Chartres, Burchard, and Liutprand.
b.s: The works held here are his editorial and critical apparatus for the Patrologia Latina volumes of Zeno of Verona, Ratherius of Verona, Leo the Great, and the canonical collections of Ivo and Burchard, including dissertations against Pseudo-Isidore, Quesnel, Baronius, Tillemont, and Petavius.

b.bio: None of The surviving records describes this Paul Baudry: they cover Balderic (Baudry), a twelfth-century monk of Liège and schoolmaster at Trier; Baudry (Balderic) of Bourgueil, abbot and archbishop/bishop of Dol (d. 1130); and Paul-Jacques-Aimé Baudry, a French painter (1828–1886). None of these wrote philological notes on Lactantius, so none can be used for this author. The library record alone identifies him: an editor whose Preface and Notes on Lactantius's De Mortibus Persecutorum occupy 127 pages of Migne's Patrologia Latina, vol. 7.
b.s: His Notes are a sustained critical commentary on Lactantius's De Mortibus Persecutorum, arguing textual points against Tollius, Maucroix, Dodwell, Columbus, and Pagi — e.g., that Lactantius is called Caecilius not Coelius, and correcting readings such as adjuvari poscunt rather than possunt.

b.bio: The name as the library prints it belongs to an author represented in Migne's Patrologia Latina (vol. 198) by a single-page dedication letter. The letter defends the order against those who denied that Premonstratensians were capable learned authors, and cites Philip, abbot of Good Hope. It should not be confused with Petrus Bellère and his successors, sixteenth- and seventeenth-century printers and publishers of Antwerp recorded in Kalliope and STCV; those men are different persons sharing the name.
b.s: The work held here is a one-page dedication letter arguing that the Premonstratensians are capable learned authors, written against those who denied the order's literary ability.

b.bio: The library's Pietro Braidi is known only through the two pieces printed under his name in Migne's Patrologia Latina 52: a long dissertation and a short preface concerning the works of St. Nicetas. None of The surviving records describes this man; they concern other persons with similar names (Pietro Braido, Pjetër/Pietro Budi, Pietro Balbi) and are not evidence for Braidi's life. His dates, nationality, and offices cannot be stated from what is at hand.
b.s: His dissertation is a sustained argument identifying Nicetas of Romatiana with Nicetas of Aquileia — denying that Gennadius's Romatian bishop or Paulinus's friend was the Dacian bishop of Remesiana — while also defending the Filioque against Zabeus and dating Nicetas before Eutychianism arose.

b.bio: the surviving records describe a different man of this name: Pierre Cally (born Ménil-Hubert-sur-Orne, died at Caen, 31 December 1709), professor of philosophy and eloquence at the University of Caen from 1660, president of the Collège des Arts from 1675, later parish priest of Saint-Martin, and a Cartesian who defended Descartes in his Universae philosophiae institutiones (Caen, 1695) and treated the Eucharist in Durand commenté (Caen, 1700). None of that career or those works match the item held here, a one-page dedication letter printed in Patrologia Latina vol. 63 that argues for restoring Christian authors to the schools against defenders of the pagan curriculum in Gaul and cites Boethius, Virgil, Cicero and Aristotle. A seventeenth-century Cartesian cannot have written a piece shelved among the Latin Fathers; the attribution to 'Pierre Cally' on the volume appears to be a homonym problem, and no source here gives dates or offices for the actual author of the letter.
b.s: The single work held under this name is a brief polemical dedication defending the place of Christian authors in education against the Gallic academies' attachment to the pagan curriculum; its true authorship is uncertain and the biographical sources attached to the name belong to someone else.

b.bio: Pierre-François Chifflet was a French Jesuit born at Besançon on 15 September 1592; he entered the Society of Jesus in 1609 and died at the collège Louis-le-Grand in Paris on 11 May 1682. He taught philosophy, Hebrew, and Scripture in Jesuit colleges, collaborated from 1624 with Héribert Rosweyde and the Bollandists, and edited patristic texts from Dijon: Fulgentius of Ruspe with Ferrandus (1649), five opuscula on the Catholic faith (1656), Paulinus of Nola (1662), Victor of Vita with Vigilius of Thapsa (1664), and an edition of Bede's Ecclesiastical History. In 1675 Colbert called him to Paris to keep the Cabinet des Médailles. The works held here are his editorial apparatus — prefaces, dissertations, and epistles — for these editions.
b.s: The pieces here are Chifflet's prefatory dissertations defending his attributions and chronologies against Baronius, Rosweyde, Bollandus, Simler, and others — notably that Victor of Vita wrote his history of the Vandal persecutions under Geiseric and Huneric in 487, dedicated it to Acacius, and also authored the Acts of the Capsa martyrs, and that Diadochus of Photice flourished in the mid-fifth century.

b.bio: None of The surviving records concerns a Pierre de la Colonge. They describe, respectively, the modern patrologist Pierre de Labriolle (1874–1940), the Benedictine Pierre Bersuire (c. 1290–1362), the Jesuit Pierre de Jarric (1566–1617), and the Cistercian Pierre de Saint-Joseph (1594–1662) — different men in different centuries and traditions, none of whom can be identified with this name. The library record shows one item under this name: a brief 'To the reader' printed in PL 192, treating prolegomena to theology and asserting that theology may be digested into a compendium from scripture. Beyond that record, nothing verifiable is asserted here about the author.
b.s: The single work held here is a prefatory piece arguing that theology may be reduced to a compendium drawn from scripture.

b.bio: Constantine was born in Syria in 664 (Wikipedia specifies Tyre) of Greek descent, the son of John, and became bishop of Rome on 25 March 708, dying there on 9 April 715. He had earlier served as a papal legate to the Third Council of Constantinople (680/681). His pontificate is remembered for his journey to Constantinople in 710/711, where he reached a compromise with Justinian II over the Trullan canons, and for upholding Roman authority against Felix, archbishop of Ravenna. He received as pilgrims King Coenred of Mercia and Offa, and Bishop Egwin of Worcester, who sought privileges for Evesham Abbey. The Catholic Encyclopedia states that the extant documents concerning Evesham bearing Constantine's name are all spurious.
b.s: The letters printed under his name in PL 89 concern privileges for Evesham Abbey — confirming royal donations, granting monastic liberty, and asserting the certainty of Egwin's Marian vision — but these documents are regarded as spurious, so they witness to Anglo-Saxon monastic claims rather than to Constantine's own authorship.

b.bio: Born at Compiègne, Coustant entered the Benedictines at Saint-Rémi, Reims, taking vows in 1672. Sent to Saint-Germain-des-Prés in 1681, he helped Thomas Blampin edit Augustine's works, distinguishing spurious from genuine writings. He then edited the works of Hilary of Poitiers and the Epistles of the Roman Pontiffs for the Maurist series. The pieces held here are his editorial apparatus: notices, dissertations and censures attached to patristic texts in Migne's Patrologia Latina, chiefly on the third-century baptismal controversy between Cyprian, Firmilian and Pope Stephen.
b.s: The works here are not free-standing treatises but the critical apparatus of a Maurist editor: dissertations and notices arguing that baptism performed by heretics is valid because its efficacy comes from Christ, not the minister — a position set against Cyprian and Firmilian and aligned with Stephen and Augustine.

b.bio: Deusdedit (also called Adeodatus I) was born in Rome around 570, the son of a subdeacon named Stephanus. He served as a priest for some forty years before his election on 19 October 615 and died in Rome on 8 November 618. His pontificate fell amid the Lombard wars; he remained loyal to Emperor Heraclius and his exarch Eleutherius, contended with an earthquake and plague in Rome, and was noted for favoring the secular diocesan clergy over monks, reversing the policy of Gregory I and Boniface IV. The first use of lead seals (bullae) on papal documents is attributed to him.
b.s: The two short texts held here — an Epistle and a Decree printed in PL 80 — are decretals treating baptismal sponsorship as a marriage impediment, the seven gifts of baptism, remarriage after separation (with recovery of dowry), and papal election with imperial legates present; the Catholic Encyclopedia notes that the few decretals ascribed to Deusdedit are unauthenticated, so readers should treat attribution with caution.

w: On the Roman Council in the case of Dionysius of Alexandria

b.bio: Dionysius was Bishop of Rome from 22 July 259 until his death on 26 December 268. A Roman presbyter under Stephen I and Sixtus II, he was elected after a nearly year-long vacancy during the Valerianic persecution, and his pontificate coincided with Gallienus's edict of toleration, which restored the Roman church's buildings and cemeteries. He reorganized the Roman church, assigning presbyters to parishes. He demanded an explanation from Dionysius of Alexandria concerning that bishop's teaching on the relation of God to the Logos after complaints from the Libyan Pentapolis; the Alexandrian synod under Dionysius satisfied him. The Antiochene synods against Paul of Samosata addressed their letter jointly to him and Maximus of Alexandria.
b.s: His surviving fragments here defend one divine nature in three distinct persons against Sabellius and Marcion, and record the Roman council that absolved Dionysius of Alexandria of doctrinal accusation — an early exercise of conciliar judgment and papal oversight in a christological controversy.

b.bio: Donus, son of a Roman named Maurice, was consecrated Bishop of Rome on 2 November 676 and died there on 11 April 678 after a reign of about seventeen months. The Liber Pontificalis records that he paved the atrium of Old St. Peter's with white marble, restored the church of St. Euphemia and repaired the Basilica of St. Paul Outside the Walls, dispersed a colony of Nestorian monks from the Syrian monastery Boetianum and gave their monastery to Roman monks, and received the obedience of Reparatus of Ravenna, ending the schism begun by Archbishop Maurus. He was already elderly at his election.
b.s: The library holds only his epitaph, a verse encomium asserting episcopal succession as the mark of the true church and the departed faithful's possession of eternal light with the fathers.

b.bio: A Roman, archpriest of S. Sabina on the Aventine before his elevation. Elected pope on 6 June 824 after a divided election in which the Roman nobility, backed by Frankish influence, prevailed over the clergy's candidate Zinzinnus. He received Lothar I in Rome and accepted the Constitutio Romana, which vested papal election in clergy and nobles under imperial confirmation, while retaining independence in matters of doctrine and discipline. He convened a Roman council in 826 against simony and untrained clergy, ordered schools at cathedral churches, and opposed the revival of Iconoclasm in the East.
b.s: The works held here are his disciplinary letters and decrees: rules on excommunication for communication with excommunicates, clerical celibacy in higher orders, restriction of laymen from ecclesiastical business, prohibition of tournaments under anathema, and reservation of violence against clergy to papal absolution.

b.bio: Eugenius III, born Bernardo near Pisa, was a Cistercian monk and abbot of the monastery of SS. Vincent and Anastasius (Tre Fontane) when elected pope on 15 February 1145, the day Lucius II died. He was the first Cistercian to become pope, a disciple of Bernard of Clairvaux, and spent much of his pontificate exiled from Rome by the rebellious commune. In 1145 he proclaimed the Second Crusade after the fall of Edessa. He died at Tivoli on 8 July 1153 and was beatified in 1872.
b.s: The library holds his letters and privileges (PL 180), which show papal government in action: protecting monastic houses, exempting monks from tithes on their own labor, and enforcing papal privilege with excommunication against bishops, counts, and chapters.

b.bio: Eutychian (Eutychianus) was bishop of Rome from January 275 until his death on 7 December 283, succeeding Felix I and followed by Caius. Born in Tuscany according to later tradition, he was buried in the catacomb of Callixtus, where fragments of his Greek epitaph were found; he was the last pope buried there. Sources agree that almost nothing else is known of him: Eusebius gives a reign of ten months, the Liber Pontificalis eight years and eleven months, and traditions about blessing field produce and burying martyrs are doubted by historians. The Exhortation to Priests printed under his name in Migne's Patrologia Latina vol. 5 treats matters — penitential canons, parish boundaries fixing tithes, thrice-yearly communion — that belong to a later period and is not accepted as his.
b.s: The single page held here is a spurious or later pastoral exhortation transmitted under his name in PL 5, valuable as evidence of how disciplinary rules were retrojected onto an early pope rather than as his own teaching.

b.bio: Formosus was probably born in Rome around 816. Nicholas I named him cardinal bishop of Porto in 864 and sent him as legate to Bulgaria; Hadrian II and John VIII later employed him on missions to France. He fell out with John VIII around 876, fled Rome, was excommunicated, and was pardoned in 878 on condition of exile. Elected pope on 6 October 891, he backed Arnulf of Carinthia against Lambert of Spoleto and died 4 April 896. The following year his successor Stephen VI had the corpse exhumed and tried — the Cadaver Synod — an episode that discredited several subsequent pontificates.
b.s: The library holds eight pages of letters and privileges under his name (PL 129), chiefly papal protections for monasteries: free abbatial election, immunity from episcopal exaction, and the rule that orders from a condemned bishop confer no grace.

b.bio: Paolo Gagliardi (Latinized Galeardus), born 1675, died 1742, was an Italian canon, jurisconsult, and poet who wrote in both Italian and Latin. He is not a Latin Father but an early modern editor of patristic texts: he prepared editions of Eusebius of Vercelli, Firmicus Maternus, and Philastrius, and of the Brescian episcopal writers Philastrius and Gaudentius, together with Rampertus and Adelmann. The works held under his name in this library are his editorial matter — prefaces and a dedication letter — to those editions, not patristic treatises of his own. A Paulus Kölner (d. 1384), a German clergyman and theologian, is a different person and is not treated here.
b.s: The works here are his prefaces and dedication to his editions of Eusebius of Vercelli (PL 12) and Firmicus Maternus and Philastrius (PL 20), which is how his name enters a patristic library.

w: On the Office of St. Gregory VII

b.bio: Prosper-Louis-Pascal Guéranger was born at Sablé-sur-Sarthe on 4 April 1805 and died at Solesmes on 30 January 1875. Ordained a priest in 1827, he acquired the priory of Solesmes in 1832 and restored Benedictine monastic life there in 1833; in 1837 the Holy See erected it as an abbey and appointed him abbot and head of the French Benedictine Congregation. An Ultramontanist opponent of Gallicanism, he campaigned for the Roman liturgy against the local French uses and wrote the fifteen-volume Liturgical Year. The work held here is his historical-polemical office for the feast of Gregory VII, defending the pope's sanctity (including posthumous miracles) and the church's liberty in the investiture contest.
b.s: The founder of the Solesmes congregation and a principal figure of the nineteenth-century liturgical movement; the work here is his defense of Gregory VII as saint and defender of ecclesiastical liberty.

w: On the Relics of SS. Bernard and Malachy

b.bio: Philippe Guignard was a French archivist-paleographer, born in Dijon (sources give 1819 or 1820), who worked at the departmental archives of the Côte-d'Or from 1840 and then served as archivist of the Aube before directing the Dijon municipal library from 1851 to 1904. He catalogued the Dijon collections, including the Cîteaux manuscripts, and edited the Monuments primitifs de la règle cistercienne (1878). The work held here, on the relics of Bernard of Clairvaux and Malachy of Armagh, is a historical study of the tombs, relic translations, and continuing pilgrimage at Clairvaux, arguing against Manrique's account.
b.s: His work here documents the medieval and early modern cult of Bernard of Clairvaux and Malachy at Clairvaux from archival and liturgical evidence.

w: Catalogues of the works of Peter of Blois
Vindications of the Dialogues of Saint Gregory

b.bio: Pierre de Goussainville (also Gussanville; Latinized Petrus Gussanvilla), born at Chartres in 1620 and died there in 1683, was a French Catholic apologist and scholar of the Gregorian reform. After theological studies he served as vicar of Sainte-Madeleine in Paris, then gave up the post to devote himself to patristic and Christian-antiquarian research. He assisted Jean-Baptiste Souchet with the edition of Yves de Chartres, edited the works of Peter of Blois (Paris, 1667) — prefaced by his Vita Petri Blesensis, first published in 1647 — and edited Gregory the Great's Opera in three volumes (1675), both dedicated to Louis de Bassompierre, bishop of Saintes. He was the first to challenge the attribution to Gregory of the Commentary on the First Book of Kings. He died in poverty.
b.s: The works held here are the paratexts of his editions: the Life of Peter of Blois, catalogues of Peter's works, and the Vindications defending the authenticity of Gregory the Great's Dialogues against critics who denied Gregory wrote them or objected to their style.

b.bio: Hilarius (also Hilarus), a native of Sardinia and archdeacon under Leo I, was elected bishop of Rome on 19 November 461 and died on 28 or 29 February 468 (sources differ). As Leo's legate at the Second Council of Ephesus in 449 he opposed the condemnation of Flavian of Constantinople and fled the violence of Dioscurus of Alexandria. His pontificate enforced canon law and settled jurisdictional disputes among bishops of Gaul and Spain. The letters held here address church order in Gaul — including disputes involving Mamertus of Vienne and Silvanus of Calahorra — and defend the authority of the apostolic see over ordination.
b.s: His letters are primary evidence for how the fifth-century Roman see asserted binding authority over episcopal appointments and canonical discipline in Gaul and Spain.

b.bio: Philipp Jaffé, born in Schwersenz near Posen and trained at Berlin under Leopold von Ranke, was a historian and philologist of the nineteenth century. His Regesta Pontificum Romanorum (Berlin, 1851), cataloguing some 11,000 papal documents to 1198, made his name. He joined the Monumenta Germaniae Historica as an editor but resigned in 1863 amid an academic conflict worsened by the antisemitism of contemporary German scholarship. The items shelved here under Latin Fathers are not patristic writings: they are Jaffé's diplomatic notices appended to Migne volumes, chiefly on the textual history of the register of Gregory VII.
b.s: The works held here are Jaffé's critical notices establishing that all printed editions of Gregory VII's register derive from Caraffa's edition, that the compiler followed a genuine register only through book seven, and that neglect of the Vatican codex corrupted every edition.

b.bio: Philippe Labbe (Philippus Labbeus), born at Bourges on 10 July 1607, entered the Society of Jesus on 28 September 1623, taught rhetoric and philosophy, and held the chair of theology for five years. He died at Paris, at the College of Clermont, 16 or 17 March 1667. A prolific writer on historical, geographical and philological questions — Sommervogel enumerates more than eighty works — he was ranked with Denis Pétau among the most notable French Jesuits in history. In the volumes here he appears as an editor and annotator of patristic material: a historical notice, a note on the Council at Trosly, and observations on manuscripts, citing Flodoard, Paul the deacon of Aquileia, Chrodegang, Jacques Sirmond and Dom Luc d'Achery.
b.s: The works held here show Labbe as a seventeenth-century Jesuit editor whose collation of ancient manuscripts underpinned his historical notices on Frankish church councils and figures such as Peretharit and Cunibert against Erlebald, count of the castricensis district.

b.t: Roman Catholic scholarly (not a patristic author)
b.bio: Peter Lambeck (Lambecius), born at Hamburg on 13 April 1628 and died at Vienna on 4 April 1680, was a German historian and librarian rather than a patristic author. Nephew and protégé of Lucas Holstenius (Holste), papal librarian, he studied at Amsterdam and Paris, took a doctorate in laws, worked in Rome under his uncle's direction, and entered the service of Emperor Leopold I as librarian and court historiographer. He is best known for his prodromus to a planned edition of the imperial library's Greek codices. The shelf here groups him with Latin Fathers, but the works held are not patristic.
b.s: The single work held is a two-page Abbreviation of the Chronicle printed in Migne's PL 104, a world chronicle computing 4,761 years from creation and 3,952 years from Adam to Christ, citing Bede; readers should treat its attribution and placement among the Fathers with caution.

b.bio: The library holds only a seven-page preface printed under this name in PL 165, and none of the sources consulted connects that preface to a specific man. Three distinct bearers of the name must be kept apart: Pietro Antonio Lazzari (1572–1630), a canonist who published practical questions on excommunication and censuses for both internal and external forums; a Pietro Lazzari recorded by the Turin archives as a collaborator of Cardinal Oppizzoni (dates unknown); and Pietro Lazzari (1895–1979), an Italian-American sculptor and painter. Nothing here establishes that the preface is by any one of them.
b.s: The single item held is a short prefatory piece in PL 165; its authorship cannot be fixed from surviving records.

w: A second notice on Peter of Riga

b.bio: Polykarp Leyser the Elder was born at Winnenden in Württemberg and died at Dresden. He was superintendent of Braunschweig, general-superintendent of the Saxon church-circle, professor of theology at Wittenberg, and chief court-preacher and consistorial councillor of Saxony. Nephew of Jakob Andreae and stepson of Lukas Osiander, he was shaped also by Martin Chemnitz, whose Loci Theologici he re-edited in 1592 and whose harmony of the Gospels he continued. His own Loci theologici (1591/92), Harmonia evangelica (1593), Postilla (1593) and De controversiis iudicium (1594) were forged in the disputes with Crypto-Calvinism in Saxony, the exorcism controversy, and Lutheran Christological debates. A dynasty of Lutheran theologians descended from him.
b.s: The single work held here is a two-page scholarly notice on Peter of Riga, arguing from manuscript and bibliographic evidence that Peter flourished about 1170, authored the Aurora, that Giles corrected and supplemented it, that its first four books alone use hexameter, that it treats the Song of Songs as non-canonical, and that the complete Aurora remained unpublished.

w: Oration for the Consecration of Marcellina

b.bio: Liberius was a Roman deacon before being consecrated bishop of Rome on 22 May 352 per the Catalogus Liberianus (probably elected 17 May), succeeding Julius I; he died in Rome on 24 September 366. His pontificate fell under the Arian emperor Constantius II. His first recorded act was to write to Constantius asking for a council at Aquileia on the case of Athanasius. He was exiled for refusing to abandon Athanasius's cause. The PL 8 material printed under his name is largely documentary and polemical: letters, imperial correspondence, and later historians' accounts (Socrates, Sozomen) that cite or argue against Liberius himself.
b.s: The works here are the letters and sayings of the pope whose exile became a test case for conciliar authority and fidelity to Nicaea under an Arian emperor.

b.bio: Marcellinus was a Roman, son of Projectus according to the Liber Pontificalis, and bishop of Rome from 30 June 296 until his death in 304 during the Diocletian persecution. The Felician Catalogue reports that he offered incense under compulsion before repenting and dying for the faith; Eusebius says the persecution caught him, while Augustine rejects the charge of apostasy. He is omitted from the Liberian Depositio lists, and his chronology is confused with that of his successor Marcellus I. Nothing of his own activity survives.
b.s: The single item held here is a four-page appendix from Migne's PL 7 printed under his name, defending sacrifice offered equally to Father and Son and assigning disputes among Christians to church courts; its citations of Hormisdas and Leo suggest a later, probably spurious compilation rather than a genuine work of this pope.

b.bio: Marcellus I succeeded Marcellinus after a vacancy of nearly three years during and after the Diocletian persecution, being elected bishop of Rome in May or June 308 under Maxentius. He found the Roman church divided over how to treat Christians who had lapsed, and imposed severe penances on them; the resulting disorder led to his banishment from Rome by Maxentius in 309, and he died the same year, succeeded by Eusebius. Damasus later placed an epitaph on his tomb recording these conflicts. No genuine writings of his survive.
b.s: The single item held under this name, Appendix II of PL 7, is a four-page polemic against Maxentius defending persecuted bishops and procedural rights at synods (persecution of bishops is persecution of Christ himself; restitution must precede a bishop's trial at a synod; no condemnation without legitimate accusers and right of defense). It cannot be the pope's own writing — it cites authors such as Leo, Jerome and Gregory — and its actual authorship and provenance are uncertain; it should not be attributed to any particular circle without further evidence.

b.bio: The name 'Marinus' as printed here does not belong to Pope Marinus I (died 15 May 884), despite the shared name and shelf placement among Latin patristic authors. The two items held under this name — a Privileges and an Epistle in PL 126 — cite King Dagobert, Eligius bishop of Noyon, and emperors Charles, Louis, and Carloman, and concern monastic privilege: monks electing their own abbot, exemption from forced hospitality dues (mansionaticum), limits on episcopal visitation, and papal confirmation of royal grants to monasteries. These are Merovingian-Carolingian monastic documents, not the correspondence of the late-ninth-century pope, whose career (legate at Constantinople, bishop of Caere) belongs to a different man.
b.s: The works here are charters and letters defending monasteries against bishops and counts who exacted mansionaticum and against abbots imposed by subreption, asserting apostolic protection and excommunication for violators of privilege.

b.bio: Marinus II was a Roman who served as cardinal-priest of San Ciriaco alle Terne before being elevated to the papacy on 30 October 942 through the intervention of Alberic II of Spoleto, during the period called the Saeculum obscurum. He died in April or May 946 and was succeeded by Agapetus II. His pontificate concentrated on administration: he worked for reform of clergy at home and abroad through legates, favoured monastic development, repaired basilicas, and cared for the poor. He is sometimes erroneously listed as Pope Martin III. The letters and privileges printed in PL 133 are a few privileges for monasteries.
b.s: The works held here are his monastic privileges: diplomas asserting that apostolic privilege protects monastery property from secular and ecclesiastical seizure, exempts monasteries from all jurisdiction save the apostolic see (including episcopal jurisdiction), confirms ancient episcopal boundaries by papal authority, and anathematizes violators until restitution — documents against Sicus of Capua and other diocesan claimants.

w: On the Life and Doctrine of Agobard

b.bio: Jean Papire Masson, born at Saint-Germain-Laval in the Forez, was a French humanist historian, geographer, biographer and jurist. He entered the Society of Jesus, taught literature in Rome and Naples, then left the order to take a chair at the collège du Plessis; he studied law under François Baudouin at Angers around 1570 and later became librarian to the Chevalier de Chiverny and avocat to the Parlement of Paris. He wrote annals of the French kings in Latin and French and defended Antoine Matharel against Hotman's Francogallia. In 1604 he discovered a manuscript of Agobard of Lyon and edited it.
b.s: The works here are his edition of Agobard of Lyon — the life and preface through which the Carolingian bishop's treatises on true worship, excommunication of Jews, and anti-Fredegisus polemic reached print.

b.bio: The name covers an anonymous community of Latin monks living on the Mount of Olives at Jerusalem around the turn of the ninth century. Their single surviving letter is addressed to Pope Leo III and the emperor Charlemagne ('Lord Charles'). In it they defend the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, assert the primacy of the Roman see, and answer objections from John, a monk of the monastery of St. Sabas. A modern study has raised the question whether the letter is instead a forgery by Adémar of Chabannes.
b.s: The letter is an early witness to Western Filioque theology argued from Jerusalem itself, directed to Leo III and Charlemagne against Greek opposition from St. Sabas.

b.bio: Latinius Pacatus Drepanius, a Gallo-Roman orator from Aginnum (Agen) educated at Burdigala (Bordeaux), flourished in the late fourth century. He was a friend of Ausonius and Symmachus. He delivered a panegyric to Theodosius I in the senate house at Rome in 389, celebrating the defeat of the usurper Maximus, received the proconsulship of Africa in 390, and is attested as comes rerum privatarum in 393. Whether he was pagan or Christian is uncertain; his speech denounces Maximus' persecution of the Priscillianists.
b.s: The panegyric held here is an important historical document beyond its flattery, containing a contemporary Latin account of Theodosius' rise, his restoration of churches from Arians to Catholics, his public penance for the Thessalonican massacre, and the victory over Maximus.

b.bio: Palladius was abbot of Saint-Germain at Auxerre and became bishop of Auxerre in 622, succeeding Desiderius. Sources agree on his charity toward the poor and his monastic foundations: he embellished the cathedral of Saint-Étienne, moved the monastery of Saint-Julien outside the walls for nuns (644), founded a monastery at Saint-Eusèbe for men, and is credited with the first annual endowment for worship. Sources differ on his death year (658, 659, or 661); he was canonized in 945 after miracles at his tomb. The library holds a single epistle under his name in PL 87.
b.s: The work held here is one epistle in PL 87; Palladius matters chiefly as a seventh-century Gallic bishop whose foundations shaped the church of Auxerre.

b.bio:
Palladius Helenopolitanus (c. 363–before 431) — Palladius was born in Galatia in 363 or 364 and took up monastic life on the Mount of Olives around 386, later visiting the Egyptian ascetics of Nitria and Kellia. He was consecrated bishop of Helenopolis in Bithynia in 400, associated with John Chrysostom at the Synod of the Oak in 403, and exiled to Egypt after defending him; there he wrote his Dialogue on the Life of Chrysostom. He returned to his diocese after 412 and died before 431, probably at Aspuna.

Hervet, Gentian (1499–1584) — Gentian Hervetus (Hervet), born at Olivet near Orléans, was a French theologian, humanist, and controversialist. After studying at Orléans he tutored in Paris, then followed Thomas Lupset to England and entered the household of Cardinal Reginald Pole in Rome, where he translated Greek Fathers into Latin, including Clement of Alexandria, John Chrysostom, Theodoret, Palladius, and Nicholas Cabasilas. He was secretary to Cardinal Cervini (later Marcellus II), accompanied him to the Council of Trent in 1546, delivered an oration there against clandestine marriages, was ordained priest in 1556, became Vicar-General of Noyon, and received a canonry at Reims, preaching against the Calvinists.
b.s: The library holds only a brief preface under his name from PL 73; his standing rests chiefly on the Lausiac History and the Dialogue on the Life of Chrysostom, major sources for early monasticism and for Chrysostom's career.

b.bio:
Pammachius (c. 340–410) — Pammachius was a Roman senator, possibly of the gens Furia, and a schoolmate of Jerome in the schools of rhetoric. He married Paulina, second daughter of Paula of Rome, in 385; after her death in 397 he put on a religious habit and gave himself up to works of charity, and with Fabiola built a hospice at Porto, at the mouth of the Tiber, for poor strangers. He was probably among those who denounced Jovinian to Pope Siricius in 390, and in 399 he and Oceanus wrote to Jerome asking him to translate Origen's De Principiis and to repudiate Rufinus's insinuations. In 401 Augustine thanked him for a letter urging the people of Numidia to abandon Donatism. Sources give his death as about 409 or 410.

Oceanus (fl. 396–399) — Oceanus was a Roman nobleman connected with Fabiola and the Julian family, and a friend and correspondent of Jerome, Augustine, and Pammachius. He probably met Jerome during Jerome's stay in Rome in 383–385. He first appears protesting against Carterius, a Spanish bishop who had remarried after baptism; around 396–397 he visited Jerome at Bethlehem with Fabiola, fleeing the Hunnish threat. Back in Rome he stood against Origenism: with Pammachius he wrote to Jerome (Ep. 83) demanding a true translation of Rufinus's edition of Origen's Peri Archon, and Tranquillinus reported to Jerome his battle with Origenist teaching (Jerome, Ep. 62). Jerome later wrote to him on Fabiola's death.
b.s: The letters held here are his correspondence with Jerome, Augustine, and Paulinus of Nola, through which he acted as Jerome's representative in Rome on questions of translation, Origenism, and the Jovinian controversy.

b.bio: Pandulf, printed here as Pandulf of Alatri (also Pandulf of Pisa; Pandulphus Aletrinus), was a twelfth-century Italian cardinal, native of Rome, and biographer of contemporary popes, nephew of Cardinal Hugo of Alatri. Under Paschal II he served as ostiarius at the papal court; Gelasius II elevated him to lector and exorcist on 10 March 1118, and Calixtus II ordained him subdeacon. He accompanied his uncle to Benevento when Gelasius fled the Frangipani in September 1118. In the schism of 1130 he supported Anacletus II against Innocent II. The library holds one work under this name: a short Life of Pope Gelasius II.
b.s: His Life of Gelasius II is an eyewitness-adjacent account of the 1118 election and flight from imperial and Frangipani violence, written to defend canonical election against Henry V's opposition — and, per recent scholarship (Veneziani & Renzi), composed during the 1130 schism as Anacletian propaganda supporting Anacletus and delegitimizing his enemies.

b.bio: Pandulf of Pisa was a twelfth-century Italian cardinal and a native of Rome, nephew of Cardinal Hugo of Alatri. Under Paschal II he served as ostiarius at the papal court; Gelasius II elevated him to lector and exorcist in 1118, and Calixtus II ordained him subdeacon. He accompanied his uncle to Benevento as rector in 1118, and appears to have witnessed the election of Gelasius II in 1118 and the election of Honorius II in 1124, judging by the detail of his biographies. In the schism after 1130 he supported Anacletus II against Innocent II; Anacletus named him cardinal-deacon of SS. Cosma e Damiano, and he signed Anacletus's bulls on 8 February 1131, 7 December 1134, and 21 March 1137.
b.s: His biographies of contemporary popes, written for the Liber Pontificalis, are near-contemporary accounts of papal elections and conflicts with antipopes such as Burdinus. Robinson notes his life of Gelasius II is inaccurate in electoral details and polemical in purpose relating to the schism of 1130. The works held here treat the Church's peace with emperor and princes, the Lateran council's restoration of peace, the defeat and imprisonment of antipope Burdinus, and the pope's compelled concessions regarding Count Roger of Sicily.

b.bio: Paphnutius of Egypt (d. 4th century) — Paphnutius of Egypt, also called Paphnutius of Thebes, was said to be an Egyptian disciple of Anthony the Great who became bishop of a city in the Upper Thebaid in the early fourth century. Under Maximinus he lost his right eye and was hamstrung for the faith and sent to the mines; at Nicaea (325) Constantine reportedly honored him as a confessor. He is credited with opposing the imposition of clerical celibacy on married clergy at that council. His historicity is disputed, and neither his see nor his death date is known.
b.s: The library holds under his name the Life of Saint Onuphrius, a short desert narrative recounting how God sustained the ascetic through angelic bread, consolation in affliction, and reward of eternal life for suffering.

b.bio: Paschalis I was bishop of Rome from 25 January 817 until his death in 824. A Roman by birth and son of Bonosus, he had been abbot of the monastery of St Stephen near St Peter's before his unanimous election on the death of Stephen IV. His pontificate dealt chiefly with relations to the Frankish empire of Louis the Pious: he obtained the Pactum Ludovicianum confirming the rights and possessions of the Holy See, and in 823 crowned Lothair I as emperor in Rome. He rebuilt several Roman basilicas, including Santa Prassede, where he was buried.
b.s: The letters held here concern papal privileges — the pallium as sign of unity with the apostolic see, perpetual confirmation of the Ravennate church's exemptions, and rulers' duty to protect vowed church property — against Lombard and simoniac abuse.

b.bio: Paschasinus was bishop of Lilybaeum in Sicily around c. 440, when Vandal raids devastated the island and Leo the Great sent him financial aid. Leo consulted him on the Paschal cycle in 443 and again in 451; his reply, De Quaestione Paschali, favors the Alexandrian Easter computation over the Roman one and recounts a yearly miracle of rising water in a baptistery font of an outlying church of his see on the true Paschal Eve. In 451 Leo sent him as one of his legates, with Lucentius of Asculum and the presbyter Bonifacius, to the Council of Chalcedon, where he seems to have held the chief place among the three legates, subscribing the acts in the pope's name before the others.
b.s: He is remembered chiefly as a leading papal legate at Chalcedon in 451 and as the author of an extant letter on the Easter reckoning.

b.bio: the surviving records describe twentieth- and twenty-first-century holders of the see of Jerusalem (Fouad Twal, Pierbattista Pizzaballa) and are homonyms of office only; they are not evidence about this author and have been set aside. What is known comes solely from the library record: a single-page Latin letter addressed to Westerners, printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 155, written in the context of the crusading movement. It invokes George, Theodore, Demetrius, and Basil, treats the Church, baptism, true worship, and predestination, and frames victory over enemies as Christ's gift rather than a matter of numbers.
b.s: The letter here is a contemporary crusade-era voice from Jerusalem itself, arguing that God grants victory to the Church's armies and that the martyr's crown is predestined from eternity.

w: On the Life of St. Martin
On the Visitation of His Nephew

b.bio: A Christian poet of the second half of the fifth century, called Petrocorius (Petricordius) in the manuscripts, from which his birthplace is inferred as Petrocorii, modern Périgueux. Nothing else about his life or parentage can be clearly made out; the praenomen 'Benedictus' sometimes given him rests on a confusion with Paulinus of Nola. Sidonius Apollinaris mentions an eminent rhetorician of Périgueux named Paulinus whom some have identified with him, but the identification is uncertain. His verse Life of Martin was written during the episcopate of Perpetuus of Tours (perhaps c. 450/470) and dedicated to that bishop.
b.s: His six-book hexameter Life of St. Martin — books 1–5 versifying Sulpicius Severus' Life and Dialogues, book 6 recounting twelve posthumous miracles at Martin's tomb drawn from a document of Bishop Perpetuus — was a significant early verse epic on Martin, adapting Sulpicius' narrative for later readers.

b.bio: The identity of this 'Paul of Constantinople' cannot be established from surviving records. Several men named Paul are attached to Constantinople in the literature — a sixth bishop of the see (d. c. 350), a Latin patriarch (d. 1371), and a Persian-born deacon said to have been a disciple of Nestorius — but none of these accounts gives dates or offices matching the work held here, so none can be identified with this author. The single work held here is a short epistle from the seventh-century monothelite controversy: it defends one will in the incarnate Christ, reads Christ's Gethsemane saying negatively rather than positively, appeals to Cyril's anathemas, invokes Sergius and Honorius alongside Chalcedon and the Fifth Synod, and rejects Nestorius, Theodore, Diodorus, Apollinaris, Eutyches, and Severus alike.
b.s: The single epistle held here is a compact specimen of monothelite argumentation, mounting dyophysite and miaphysite opponents together on one side and resting its case on councils and fathers alone.

w: On the Life of the Fathers of Mérida

b.bio: Paul was a deacon of Mérida in Visigothic Spain, active in the late sixth and early seventh century, writing in Latin. He is not the mid-sixth-century Greek metropolitan bishop of Mérida of the same name, whose career is recorded separately, and should not be confused with Paul the Deacon, author of the Historia Langobardorum. His one surviving work, the Vitas Patrum Emeritensium (On the Life of the Fathers of Mérida), narrates the five bishops of that see from Paul to Renovatius, with the longest treatment given to Masona. Composition is generally dated to the seventh century, though some scholars argue for as late as the ninth; Javier Arce holds it was written under Bishop Stephen (633–638) and finally compiled by deacon Paul under Festus (672–680). His death is dated only uncertainly to 650.
b.s: His history is a major source for the Visigothic Kingdom of Toledo and for the conflict between the Catholic and Arian churches that ended in the conversion of the Visigoths from Arianism.

b.bio: Paul of Verdun, of a wealthy Gallo-Roman family, was educated at the court of Chlothar II alongside the future king Dagobert I, Desiderius of Cahors, and Eligius. He became a hermit on a hill near Trier later called Paulsberg, then joined the monastery of Tholey, where he taught in its school and is said to have served as second abbot. Dagobert I made him bishop of Verdun around 630, reportedly against his will, through the influence of his former student Adalgisel Grimo. He is said to have been a brother of Germanus of Paris, though Germanus's Vita makes no mention of this. Sources disagree on his death date: Wikipedia gives 647 or 648, Butler's Lives gives 631, Catholic Online gives 649.
b.s: The library holds letters under his name (PL 87), which cite Desiderius, documenting the network of Merovingian court-educated bishops.

b.bio: The library holds one short epistle under the name 'Paul the Perfidious' in Migne's Patrologia Latina 96. None of The surviving records identifies an author by this name. They describe three distinct figures who must not be confused with him: Paul the Deacon (Paulus Diaconus), the Lombard historian and Benedictine monk of Monte Cassino of the late eighth century; Paulinus of Nola, the fourth-century bishop and Latin poet; and Paul the Persian, a sixth-century Syriac writer on Aristotelian logic who reportedly converted to Zoroastrianism. Nothing about the life, office, or dates of the author printed here is established by these sources.
b.s: The work held here is a single-page epistle treated as exegesis; its attribution to any known Paul remains unverified.

b.bio: Pelagius I was a Roman of noble family, son of John, a civic official. As a deacon he accompanied Pope Agapetus I to Constantinople in 536 and served as apocrisiarius there under Vigilius, gaining the confidence of Emperor Justinian I. He initially opposed Justinian's condemnation of the Three Chapters but later accepted it. Elected pope on 16 April 556 as Justinian's candidate — an appointment poorly received in the West — he governed until his death on 3 March 561. His pontificate was consumed by the schism that followed the Fifth General Council.
b.s: The letters held here are instruments of that post-Chalcedonian reconciliation: they defend coercion of schismatics as an act of love, insist that separation from the apostolic see is itself schism, and require imperial approval for episcopal ordination — against the bishops of Liguria, Venetia, and Istria and their leader Eufrasius.

b.bio: Peringer of Tegernsee is known to this library only through three pages of letters printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina 141 under his name. The letters are legal and administrative documents concerning Tegernsee Abbey in Bavaria: petitions and polemics on behalf of the monastery against named opponents (Tagininus, Count Diemo, Wezilin and Pezilin, Penno), citing its patron saint Quirinus, a king, and a duke. the surviving records here describe other Tegernsee monks — Metellus, Werner, Anton Pelchinger — none identified with Peringer, so nothing further about his life can be asserted.
b.s: The letters held here record how a twelfth-century imperial abbey pursued restitution of lands and benefices through royal promise and formal judgment rather than armed force.

b.bio: Perpetuus came from the senatorial family that produced his predecessor Eustachius and his successor Volusianus. Appointed about 460, he led the church of Tours for thirty years, presided over a council at Tours shortly after his elevation and the Council of Vannes in 465, and disciplined clergy he judged unworthy. He built churches and monasteries and replaced Saint Britius's chapel over Martin's tomb with a basilica (c. 470). Britannica credits him with instituting a pre-Christmas fast from St. Martin's Day (11 November), later known as St. Martin's Lent.
b.s: The library holds only his Testament, a will whose provisions — manumitted slaves serving the church freely, debts to the dying remitted as alms, endowed revenues for perpetual lights at saints' tombs, burial near the saint until judgment — are a primary document of Gallic piety and church property in the late fifth century.

b.bio: Pierre Amiel de Sarcenas (Petrus Amelii), a Benedictine (O.S.B.) born at Sarcenas in the diocese of Grenoble (birth year uncertain), served as Archbishop of Vienne (27 April 1362), Naples (9 January 1363) and Embrun (5 September 1365) before being created Cardinal-Priest of San Marco on 18 December 1378, shortly after the election of Urban VI; he is listed as a pseudocardinal of the Avignon line and died at Avignon on 10 August 1389, buried in the Celestine church there. He must not be confused with the earlier Pierre Amiel, Archbishop of Narbonne (1226–1245), who fought Catharism under Louis VIII.
b.s: The works held here are his account of the solemn papal liturgy — the Roman Order XV with its additions — a historical description of papal ceremonial under Urban VI, covering advent and lenten usages, the pope's vestments and movements at mass, communion discipline (the celebrant alone communicates at solemn papal mass), and disputes over feasts (transferred off advent and lent sundays) and mass offerings.

b.bio: Anastasius Bibliothecarius, born about 810, was a nephew of Bishop Arsenius of Orte and learned Greek from Eastern monks, making him among the most learned ecclesiastics of ninth-century Rome. He became cardinal priest of St. Marcellus about 848, was deposed in 853 for political activity, and stood briefly as antipope against Benedict III in 855 before being reconciled. Under Nicholas I he served as abbot of Santa Maria in Trastevere and ghost-wrote much papal correspondence; Adrian II appointed him librarian of the Roman Church, and in 869 he went to Constantinople as envoy of Emperor Louis II, arriving during the Eighth Ecumenical Council.
b.s: The works held here present him as a compiler of Frankish history and relic narratives: an abbreviated history of the Franks asserting that papal authority may depose and appoint kings and that Charles Martel was damned for despoiling the church, and an account of the translation of St. Stephen defending relics that expel demons and work healing miracles.

b.bio: Peter Chrysolanus (Pietro Grossolano), an Italian prelate born in the later eleventh century, held a minor see before being raised to the archbishopric of Milan in 1110. Pope Paschal II sent him on a mission to the Byzantine emperor Alexius I Comnenus, where he took part in the controversy over the procession of the Holy Spirit. He died in 1117. The name is sometimes confused with the fifth-century bishop Peter Chrysologus, a different man.
b.s: The work held here, his oration to Emperor Alexius I Comnenus on the Holy Spirit, is a Latin polemic defending the filioque against Greek objections, arguing that denial of the Spirit's procession from the Son diminishes the Son's glory and that equal mission entails equal procession.

b.bio: Surviving records do not clearly identify this author; they concern other men named Peter or Bernard of Clairvaux, and none gives dates for him. The library's six pages of letters identify the writer as a monk of Clairvaux writing within Bernard's circle: he cites Bernard most often, addresses 'the fathers of the order,' and writes petitions and polemics against the elevation of one Henry to the bishopric of Toulouse, against the lord of York, and against any pope or king consenting to Henry's promotion. His themes are charity that spends itself for others, patience under temptation permitted for greater glory, and public punishment of the murderer who deserves no pardon.
b.s: The letters held here are evidence of Clairvaux's intervention in two episcopal disputes—Toulouse and York—in Bernard's generation.

b.bio: The library holds one page under this name, printed in PL 139: a text on an oath of fidelity owed by an abbot to his metropolitan church of Ravenna, citing Benedict's rule and Gerbert as archbishop of Ravenna. None of The surviving records concerns this author; they describe Peter of Blois, Peter Comestor, and Peter Cellensis — different men with different bodies of work — so nothing from them is used here. No source gives dates, birthplace, or office for a Peter of Classe.
b.s: The single held page is a historical document asserting that a monastic superior is bound by oath to his metropolitan see at Ravenna, that his office requires observance of Benedict's rule, and that church property may be alienated only by renewing leases.

w: Deeds of the Abbots of Bec

b.bio: Peter of Dive (Petrus de Diva) is known to this library only through a single work held under his name in PL 181. the surviving records describe other men — Petrus Divaeus (1535–1581), a Leuven antiquary and city pensionary, and the scholastic Peters Comestor, of Blois, and of Poitiers — none of whom wrote on Bec; they are different persons and are set aside. No source or record here gives dates, offices, or places for Peter of Dive himself.
b.s: His Gesta abbatum Beccensium preserves the history of Bec's abbots — Herluin and Lanfranc above all — presenting monastic conversion, discipline, and reform as works of divine grace.

b.bio:
Peter Leonis (d. 2 June 1128) — Pier Leoni (Petrus Leonis), son of Leo de Benedicto and grandson of a Jewish banker of Rome baptized as Benedictus Christianus, was the most powerful man in early twelfth-century Rome. A consul of the city and one of its regents during Paschal II's absence in 1108, he led the legation that negotiated with Henry V in 1111 and restored Pope Gelasius II to freedom after Cencio Frangipane imprisoned him in 1118. He controlled the Tiber Island, the Theatre of Marcellus, and Castel Sant'Angelo, and Urban II died in his fortified house near S. Nicola in Carcere. His sons included Peter Pierleoni, cardinal deacon by 1113 and later antipope Anacletus II, who bore the same name.

Gregory the Legate (unknown) — The library holds one page of letters under the name 'Gregory the Legate' (PL 166). The letters are legal-judicial documents concerning the monastery of Montreuil and a dispute with Wido the knight: they assert that altars rightfully belong to their founding monastery, that a prior judgment voids a later donation, that an absolute donation precludes subsequent donation, and that landlord consent is required for transferring tenants. None of The surviving records identifies this correspondent; they describe other Gregories (Gregory of Ostia, d. 1044; Gregorio di Montelongo, c. 1200–1269) or the legatine office generally, and none mentions Montreuil or these letters. He is therefore treated here only as what the record shows: a papal legate named Gregory who adjudicated property disputes involving Montreuil.
b.s: The work held here is a letter adjudicating a dispute with Wido the knight over altars claimed by the monastery of Montreuil, asserting that prior judgment voids later donation and that absolute donation precludes subsequent transfer.

w: On the Antiquity and Improvement of the Island of Maillezais

b.bio: A Benedictine monk of Maillezais Abbey in Bas-Poitou, writing under Abbot Goderannus (abbot from 1060, bishop of Saintes from 1067), at whose request he wrote. His chronicle Qualiter fuit constructum Malliacense monasterium, on the abbey's foundation and the translation of Saint Rigomer, is now dated to about 1060 or 1070 and is classed by modern scholars as a monastic foundation legend. Older references call him abbot; the sources here do not confirm that office. He also edited Baldric of Dol's Historiae Hierosolymitanae libri IV.
b.s: The work held here is the founding history of Maillezais Abbey: it argues that divine providence founded and repeatedly restored the monastery, that ruined altars attest an earlier church on the site, and it answers opponents including Boso, count of La Marche.

b.bio: Petrus Mallius was active in the twelfth century and wrote a description of the old and new Vatican basilica. The Online Books Page lists him only as 'active 12th century' with the Descriptio Vaticanae basilicae among his works; no birth or death dates are given in the sources. He is distinct from Flavius Mallius Theodorus, the late-fourth-century Roman senator and author of De metris, from Peter Comestor (d. 1178), the French theological writer, and from Peter of Pisa (744–799), the grammarian at Charlemagne's court. The excerpts held here record the customs and rights of St. Peter's: weekly service by seven cardinal priests at Peter's altar, eighteen diaconates under an archdeacon, lamp counts, candle customs at Peter's feast, and the division of altar offerings among clergy.
b.s: His work is a primary witness to twelfth-century liturgical practice and property arrangements inside the Vatican basilica.

b.bio: The single work held under this name is a short history and polemic of Pope Paschal II's pontificate, printed in PL 163. It cannot be attributed from the available reference sources to the better-known Peter of Pisa, the Italian grammarian, deacon and poet at Charlemagne's court (d. before 799), who wrote grammars, poems, and Quaestiones in Danielem prophetam; no source given here attributes a Life of Paschal II to him. No dates can be asserted for the author of the Life of Paschal II.
b.s: The work defends Paschal II as true pope against Henry V and the antipopes Guibert, Albert, Theodoric, and Maginulf, arguing that papal election comes from God, that Guibert was never a true pope but a heresiarch, that the devil cannot confer the true pontificate, and that usurpers of the papal see fall by divine judgment.

b.bio: Peter of San Crisogono is identified by his titular church in Rome (San Crisogono). The library holds under his name three pages of letters in PL 199 directed against the Cathars and against Raymond and Bernard, associates of the bishop of Poitiers, addressed to the lord pope and to the archbishops of Bourges and Narbonne and the bishop of Toulouse. On that evidence he belongs to the twelfth- or thirteenth-century anti-Cathar polemic; no retrieved source gives his dates, office, or biography.
b.s: His letters here are a contemporary record of how church authorities handled Catharism: free hearing of heretics without coercion, expulsion of the unrepentant from Christian lands, mercy offered to repentant converts, and a defense of lawful oaths.

b.bio:
Peter of Sully (unknown) — No surviving record describes a 'Peter of Sully.' The attached sources concern Maurice de Sully (d. 1196) and Eudes de Sully (d. 1208), Bishops of Paris — different men who share the family name, and neither matches the work held under this name; they cannot be used for this author's biography. The library record alone identifies the author here: a Latin writer whose single-page text in PL 162 is a historical account of monks renouncing claims to the possessions of one Robert, preferring to suffer injury than litigate.

Robert of Arbrissel (c. 1045/1047 – 1116/1117) — Robert of Arbrissel was born at Arbrissel near Retiers in Brittany (sources give c. 1045 or c. 1047) and died at Orsan Priory (1116 per Wikipedia; probably 1117 per the Catholic Encyclopedia). He studied in Paris during the pontificate of Gregory VII, perhaps under Anselm of Laon, and from 1089 served as archpriest of Rennes under Bishop Sylvester de la Guerche. After Sylvester's death in 1093 he left the diocese, became a hermit in the forest of Craon in 1095, and then became an itinerant preacher; in 1096 he founded the double monastery of Fontevraud. His life is known chiefly from two vitae by men who knew him, Baudri of Dol and Andreas. The work held here is a short record concerning a dispute over his possessions, in which monks relinquish their claims to them.
b.s: The work held here is a brief historical notice of monastic forbearance — monks relinquishing claims to Robert's possessions on the principle that enduring injury is better than litigation — citing Ralph, Archbishop of Tours, and Peter, Bishop of Poitiers.

b.t: Latin chronicler of the First Crusade
b.bio: Peter Tudebode was a Poitevin priest, born at Civray near the start of the eleventh century, who took the cross in 1096 with Hugues de Lusignan and marched with the army of Raymond of Saint-Gilles. His two brothers died in the East. He was present at Nicaea and the siege of Antioch (1097–1098) and at the taking of Jerusalem in 1099; McClintock and Strong report his death at the close of that year. His Historia de Hierosolymitano itinere is an eyewitness narrative closely related to the anonymous Gesta Francorum — scholars dispute whether it derives from the Gesta or from a lost common source.
b.s: The work held here is a firsthand account of the First Crusade that frames the campaign as holy war: plundering fellow Christians as sin, death in battle against the Turks as martyrdom for Christ, and victory as God's gift to faithful soldiers.

b.bio: The library holds one short exegetical work under this name, Questions on Daniel (PL 96), a set of questions on the biblical Daniel treating the four-kingdom statue, the ram as the last Persian king, the he-goat as Alexander, three kinds of diviners, and answers to Porphyry's objections, citing Josephus, Eusebius, Africanus, and Greek and Latin histories. None of The surviving records describes an author matching this name and these works: they concern Peter the Deacon of Monte Cassino (12th century), Thomas the Archdeacon of Split (13th century), and Peter Lombard — all different figures with different corpora. No source gives dates, offices, or biographical details for the author of the Questions on Daniel.
b.s: The work here is a brief patristic-era question-and-answer commentary defending the traditional reading of Daniel's visions against Porphyry's attack on the book's authenticity.

w: Foundation of the College of 10 Clementine Clerics

b.bio: Pierre de Colmieu (Petrus de Collemedio), archbishop of Rouen and later cardinal, died in 1253. Biblissima records his death year and a birth no earlier than 1101; it cites the Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani article on Pietro da Collemezzo as a bibliographical reference. He should not be confused with Guido de Collemedio, bishop of Cambrai (d. 1306), a separate figure who shares the family name. The work held here is a foundation text of 1245 establishing a college of ten clerics at Albano.
b.s: The single work here is a legal-ecclesiastical document showing how an endowed clerical college was structured: stipends conditional on attendance at canonical hours, forfeitures reserved for pious uses, perpetual lamps or alms to the poor, and anniversary masses for founders' souls.

w: Letter to C., Dean of the Church of Noyon

b.bio: The library prints this name as 'Peter of Roya' and holds one work under it, a letter to C., dean of the church of Noyon (PL 194). None of the surviving records describes an author of this name; they cover Peter of Blois, Peter Comestor, and Peter of Eboli, all different men, so they cannot be used to establish any fact about this author. Nothing else can be asserted about him.
b.s: The single held item is a letter to C., dean of the church of Noyon, printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 194; its content is not described in the record.

b.bio: Philip I, son of Henry I and Anne of Kiev, was crowned co-king at Reims in 1059 and reigned as King of the Franks from 1060 until his death at Melun on 29 July 1108. His long reign saw a modest recovery of the royal domain, including the addition of the Vexin and Bourges. In church affairs his reputation was poor: he repudiated Bertha of Frisia for Bertrada of Montfort in 1092, was excommunicated by Urban II at Clermont in 1095, and resisted papal intervention in episcopal elections. Ivo of Chartres opposed him; the works here show Ivo also acting as a counselor whose authority he invoked.
b.s: The library holds not theological treatises but royal charters: diplomas granting monasteries privileges and lands 'for the redemption of the soul,' protecting church goods from death levies, freeing dependents, entrusting a decayed abbey to reformed monks, and letters in which the pope's authority reconciles an excommunicate king — documents showing how a reform-era monarch negotiated with bishops like Ivo of Chartres, Daimbert of Sens, and Pope Paschal II.

b.bio: Philip II Augustus, son of Louis VII and Adela of Champagne, reigned as King of France from 1180 until his death at Mantes in 1223. He took part in the Third Crusade alongside Richard I of England before the two quarreled in Palestine, and his later defeat of a Plantagenet-led coalition at Bouvines in 1214 broke Angevin power and made the French crown dominant in western Europe. He was the first French monarch to style himself 'King of France' rather than 'King of the Franks'. The library holds one short letter of his, printed in PL 209, concerning a levy of crusade tithes.
b.s: The letter here is a royal act defending a one-time crusade tithe as valid by consent of churches and princes while denying that it sets any precedent — evidence of how crusade finance was negotiated between throne and clergy.

b.bio: Philip the Priest (Philip the Presbyter) is known chiefly through Gennadius of Marseilles' De Viris Illustribus (c. 62), which calls him a disciple of Jerome and says he died in 456, in the reigns of Marcian and Avitus. Gennadius credits him with a Commentary on Job and with Familiar Letters, now lost. The Commentary on Job, addressed to Nectarius, circulated for centuries under other names — printed at Basle in 1527 as Philip's, but also among the works of Bede and Jerome; Cave, Oudin and Vallarsi ascribe it to Philip, though Vallarsi is less decided.
b.s: His one surviving work, the Commentary on Job held here (PL 53), is an early Latin exegesis of Job transmitted under Jerome's and Bede's names.

b.bio:
Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE–50 CE) — Philo of Alexandria was a Greek-speaking Jewish philosopher of a prominent Alexandrian family, the leading representative of Hellenistic Judaism. Sources give differing dates: Britannica has him born 15–10 BCE and dying 45–50 CE; the Catholic Encyclopedia says born about 25 BCE; Schaff's encyclopedia gives about 20 BCE to about 42 CE. The one datable event in his life is his leadership of an Alexandrian Jewish delegation to Caligula in 40 CE after anti-Jewish strife in the city. He wrote in Koine Greek, reading the Septuagint through Platonic and Stoic philosophy. The single work held under his name here, the Book of Hebrew Names (PL 23), is not by him: it is a Latin etymological lexicon of biblical names compiled by Jerome, who drew on Philo among other authorities.

Jerome of Stridon (c. c. 340–420) — Jerome (Eusebius Sophronius Hieronymus) was born at Stridon, a town on the confines of Dalmatia and Pannonia; sources give his birth between about 340-2 and 347. He was educated at Rome and baptized there (probably around 360, or about 366 per Benedict XVI), lived as an ascetic in the desert of Chalcis (374-379), was ordained priest at Antioch, spent 382-385 in Rome in close association with Pope Damasus, then settled at Bethlehem in 386, where he died on 30 September 420. He learned Hebrew and produced a Latin Bible translated from the Hebrew rather than the Septuagint (the Vulgate), commentaries, polemical essays, and historical work.
b.s: Readers meet Philo here only as a source behind Jerome's Book of Hebrew Names, a lexicon explaining the meanings of Hebrew proper names that medieval exegetes used constantly.

b.bio: Surviving records do not clearly identify this author; they concern other persons bearing the name Philotheus (a 20th-century Franciscan scholar and a 14th-century Byzantine patriarch) and are set aside as inapplicable. The library holds a six-page encomiastic poem from PL 185 praising Bernard of Clairvaux as divinely appointed to restore a decayed monastic religion, invoking Benedict and his rule, Moses, and Pope Eugene, and contrasting Bernard with pagan heroes of antiquity. The poet's identity, dates, and offices are not established by the material at hand.
b.s: The single work here is a brief Latin verse panegyric presenting Bernard of Clairvaux as heaven-sent restorer of the church, useful chiefly as evidence of the cult of Bernard among his contemporaries.

b.bio: Photius was born at Constantinople; sources place his birth variously around 810, c. 815, c. 820, or not much earlier than 827, and his death on 6 February in 893 or 897. A layman from a family tied to the patriarchs Tarasius and John VII, he was raised to the patriarchate in 858 when Emperor Michael III forced out Ignatius, held office twice (858–867, 877–886), and led the conflict with Rome over papal jurisdiction and the Filioque known as the Photian schism. He is also credited as a central figure in the conversion of the Slavs and as the leading intellect of the ninth-century Byzantine renaissance.
b.s: The single page this library holds under his name is an ascetic-exegetical piece treating unceasing attentive prayer, continence extending beyond food to the soul's movements, freedom of good works from vainglory, the prohibition on judging others, and the spiritual profit of stillness (hesychia), citing Anthony the Great, Hesychius of Jerusalem, Heraclius, and the Limonarium.

b.bio: Pibo (Pippo, Pibon), a Saxon and canon of Halberstadt, was chancellor of Henry IV in 1068 before becoming bishop of Toul (1069 or 1070 to his death in 1107). Accused of simony, he kept his see with imperial backing; he signed the renunciation of obedience to Rome at the Synod of Worms in 1076, fled Utrecht rather than witness Gregory VII's excommunication, and was reconciled at the diet of Tribur by legate Altmann of Passau. After a pilgrimage to the Holy Land and retirement at Saint-Bénigne of Dijon, Urban II ordered him back to office.
b.s: The works held here are not treatises but charters and letters: diplomas endowing monastic prayer and defending local church liberty against Duke Theodoric, Countess Sophia, and other exactors, plus a letter to Pope Paschal — documents showing how an imperial bishop used written records and synodal judgment to secure church property.

b.bio:
Pepin the Short (c. 714–768) — Pepin the Short, son of Charles Martel, was Mayor of the Palace of the Franks from 741, first jointly with his brother Carloman, and King of the Franks from 751 until his death at St Denis on 24 September 768. Educated by the monks of St Denis, he supported Boniface's reform of the Frankish church and was anointed king (first by St Boniface and then) by Pope Stephen II after deposing Childeric III. The works held under his name in PL 96 are diplomas and capitularies: royal acts regulating synods, clerical discipline, church property, and relations between bishops, priests, and counts.

Charlemagne (unknown) — The library prints these eleven volumes under the name Charlemagne. None of The surviving records gives biographical data for him directly, so no dates or offices are asserted here. The largest theological item, On Images (PL 98), corresponds to the Libri Carolini, a treatise on sacred images which modern scholarship attributes most probably to Theodulf of Orléans, bishop during the reign of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, rather than to the king's own hand (source:3). The remaining items—capitularies, privileges, diplomas, letters—are royal acts and correspondence as gathered in Migne.
b.s: The documents here show a Frankish king legislating for the church — annual synods, restoration of ecclesiastical property, subjection of priests to bishops — making them primary evidence for how Carolingian royal authority shaped canonical order.

b.bio: The name as printed collides with two different popes. the surviving records describe Pius VI (Giovanni Angelo Braschi), pope from 15 February 1775 to 29 August 1799, born at Cesena, who condemned the French Revolution and died a prisoner at Valence. But the library holds his single work in Patrologia Latina volume 57, which collects sixth-century material; an eighteenth-century pope cannot have written there. The epistle shelved under this name therefore belongs to an earlier pope bearing the same regnal title, most plausibly one of the late fifth- or sixth-century pontiffs whose letters fill that volume; the sources given do not identify which.
b.s: The single epistle held here is a brief sixth-century papal letter in PL 57; it is not the work of the eighteenth-century Pius VI described in the sources.

b.bio: Polemius Silvius was a fifth-century Christian official in the imperial administration of Gaul, active in the southeast and a friend of Hilary of Arles. Around 448–449 he composed an annotated Julian calendar (also called a laterculus or fasti), dedicated to Eucherius, bishop of Lyon. The work revised the traditional Roman festival calendar for Christian use: it removed festivals regarded as pagan, added Christian holy days where few fixed feasts yet existed, and filled gaps with meteorological markers, seasonal notes, Egyptian days, lists of emperors and provinces, and remarks on weights, measures, and grammar. He probably consulted the Calendar of Filocalus.
b.s: His calendar is a primary witness to how mid-fifth-century Gaul replaced the Roman festival cycle with Christian observance; the library holds it as the Ancient Calendar and the Laterculus or Index of Feasts, the latter recording among its theses that Christ suffered at the spring equinox.

b.bio:
Polycarp (69–155) — Polycarp was bishop of Smyrna and an Apostolic Father; Irenaeus, Tertullian, and Jerome report that he was a disciple of John the Apostle. He wrote the Epistle to the Philippians and died a martyr at Smyrna around 155, according to the letter of the Smyrnaeans. The work held here under his name, however, a chain (catena) of patristic excerpts on the four Gospels printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 68, cannot be from this second-century Greek bishop: it is Latin, exegetical, and centuries later. It belongs to a later writer or compiler circulating under the name Polycarp, and should be read as such.

Victor of Capua (d. 554) — Victor of Capua is known only through his epitaph and his writings. He became bishop of Capua in February 541 and died in April 554 after an episcopate of thirteen years; the Roman Martyrology commemorates him on 17 October as distinguished for learning and holiness.
