His best-known work is the Codex Fuldensis, one of the oldest manuscripts of the Vulgate, which he directed, revised, and corrected; it replaces the four Gospels with a single harmony which he attributed, with some doubt, to Tatian. The library holds his Interpretation of Gospel Harmonies under his name in PL 68.
b.s: The historical Polycarp matters as a link to the apostolic age, but the library's single held work is a later pseudo-Polycarpian Gospel catena treating Christology, the harmony of the evangelists' openings, martyrdom of intention, and reward.

b.bio: Pontianus was a sixth-century bishop from an African diocese (which one is not recorded) who became involved in the Three-Chapter Controversy. In 544–545 Emperor Justinian sought his signature on an edict condemning Theodore of Mopsuestia and others; Pontianus replied with a letter refusing, arguing that writings unknown to him could be rejected without condemning their authors' persons, that judgment of the dead belongs to God alone — 'what cause have we to enter into a war with the dead, where there is no victory?' — and that Chalcedon's stand against Eutychianism must not be undermined. The letter survives in Migne's Patrologia Latina 67 (pp. 996–997).
b.s: His letter to Justinian (PL 67) is a rare African episcopal protest against posthumous condemnation in the Three-Chapter Controversy, defending Chalcedon while resisting Justinian's edict.

b.bio: Pons of Melgueil, printed here as Pons of Cluny, was the seventh Abbot of Cluny, succeeding Hugh of Semur in 1109 and holding the office until 1122. Born into a noble Languedoc family long allied with the Gregorian reform, he was a nephew and godson of Pope Paschal II, an oblate at Saint-Pons-de-Thomières before taking vows at Cluny. His abbacy continued Hugh's policies: building Cluny III, expanding the order into northern France and England, and mediating the Investiture Controversy. Gelasius II named him a possible successor before dying at Cluny in 1119; Callixtus II instead made him a cardinal-deacon in January 1120. His government drew public protest from the bishop of Mâcon and archbishop of Lyon in 1119.
b.s: The works held here are his Statutes for the order and the Pious Precepts, which set out the Cluniac doctrine of posthumous suffrage: trentals of masses, monks' prayers extending to benefactors, alms to the poor as aid to souls after death, and commemoration of benefactors.

w: Letter to the Abbot of Chaumes

b.bio: No surviving record identifies a 'Pons of Saint-Ruf.' The sources describe two other figures: Lietbertus, abbot of Saint-Ruf in the diocese of Avignon from 1100 to 1110, author of the Flores Psalmorum and the Liber ecclesiastici et canonici ordinis; and Pons of Melgueil (c. 1075–1126), seventh abbot of Cluny from 1109 to 1122. Neither matches the name as printed, so their biographical details cannot be attributed to this author. The library's record shows only that a letter to the Abbot of Chaumes circulates under this name in PL 163, treating Christian liberty, faith, grace, true worship, sanctification, and moral virtue.
b.s: The single work held here is a one-page letter to the Abbot of Chaumes on Christian liberty, faith, grace, worship, sanctification, and virtue; its author cannot be further identified from the sources given.

w: On the Life and Passion of Cyprian

b.bio: Pontius was a deacon of the church at Carthage who served Cyprian and accompanied him into exile at Curubis. The only ancient notice of him is a line in Jerome's De viris illustribus (68), which credits him with a book on Cyprian's life and passion; the work itself is anonymous in transmission but is identified with Jerome's description. He writes partly from what he witnessed himself or heard from older Christians, and his preface shows he knew of no earlier account of Cyprian's martyrdom.
b.s: His Vita Cypriani is the earliest biography of Cyprian and the primary eyewitness narrative of his exile and martyrdom, prefixed to editions of Cyprian's works.

b.bio: Pierre Pons appears in this library only as the author of three pages of dedication letters printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 115). The letters accompany an edition of the writings of Eulogius of Córdoba, which Pons says were recovered by God's providence and edited by Ambrosio de Morales on behalf of the bishop. He addresses Emperor Charles V and King Philip II, urging that the saints' writings be published and that Córdoba's citizens venerate their martyrs through Eulogius's works. No biographical details of this Pons are established by the sources consulted.
b.s: His letters document how Eulogius's account of the Córdoba martyrs reached print in early modern Spain, framed as providential recovery of an ancient codex.

b.bio: Poppo was bishop of Metz from his attestation in 1090 until his death in exile in France in 1103; some records give the end of his episcopate as 1104. The works held under his name are diplomas and letters to Lambert concerning Gorze Abbey and its advocate Wezelo: they defend the abbot's jurisdiction over relics, excommunication, ministerials, investitures, and revenues against the advocate's claims.
b.s: His diplomas here are a record of an eleventh-century bishop defending monastic immunity and jurisdiction against a lay advocate, with theses on relic translation, intercession of saints, and the abbot's sole possession of the ban.

b.bio: Poppo von Babenberg, son of Leopold I of Austria and Richardis of Sualafeldgau, was educated at Regensburg and made first provost of the new cathedral at Bamberg by Emperor Henry II in 1007. When Archbishop Megingod died in 1015, Henry II selected Poppo as his successor; he was consecrated by Erkanbald of Mainz and confirmed by Pope Benedict VIII in 1016. Between 1028 and 1030 he travelled to the Holy Land with the monk Symeon of Trier; later he had Symeon buried in the Porta Nigra and on his word Pope Benedict IX canonised him. From 1037 until his death he was occupied extending Trier Cathedral westward, and died on 16 June 1047 while inspecting the construction.
b.s: The library holds an Epistle to Benedict IX under this name (PL 141), a document relevant to early medieval papal canonization practice.

b.bio: A Latin poet of the age of Constantine the Great, possibly a native of Africa. He had been banished for reasons not stated in the sources; his panegyric to Constantine, presented around the emperor's Vicennalia (326 by Smith's reckoning), won his recall — Jerome dates the restoration to 328. He has been identified with the Publilius Optatianus who was praefectus urbi in 329 and 333. Twenty-eight poems survive under his name, twenty of them forming the panegyric collection, together with Constantine's complimentary reply and the poet's letter of thanks. Though classed on this shelf with the Latin Fathers, he is a court poet, not a Christian writer.
b.s: The works held here are the panegyric and its accompanying letter to Constantine: formally ingenious pattern poems — letter squares with rubricated hidden verses, versus anacyclici readable backwards without loss of sense or metre, reciprocal hexameters yielding pentameter unchanged — praising Constantine as a just, pious ruler renewing a golden age.

b.bio: Potamius, a Spaniard, was the first recorded bishop of Lisbon and the second earliest Christian prose writer of the Iberian Peninsula after Hosius of Corduba. He emerges into history in the mid-350s under Constantius II, whose preferred theology he initially supported: he took part in the Council of Sirmium in 357 and is believed to have helped draft its creed. By the time of Ariminum (359) his position had apparently shifted; he apparently wrote to Athanasius a letter of anti-Arian polemic on the consubstantiality of the Son. After that he disappears from view.
b.s: The work held here is a short anti-Arian treatise (PL 8) asserting against the Arians that the Son is one substance with the Father, that sender and sent share one divine substance, and that the Father's greater-ness is order, not inequality of substance.

w: Laws for the Correction of Morals

b.bio: The library prints this name for the anonymous compiler of the Leges Northumbrensium Presbyterorum ('Laws of the Northumbrian Priests'), a short collection of ecclesiastical regulations preserved in a Corpus Christi College, Cambridge manuscript and dated by Documenta Catholica Omnia to roughly 900–1000. The author is unknown ('Auctor Incertus'); the title 'Presbyteres Northumbrenium' designates the work's subject matter — rules binding priests in Northumbria — not a known individual. Nothing beyond the manuscript and Migne's printing (PL 138, cols. 521–526A) is recorded about who compiled it.
b.s: The single work held here is a brief penitential-disciplinary code regulating priestly conduct: baptism of infants within nine days, restrictions on mass (consecrated altar, chalice, wine, limited frequency), prohibition on priests purchasing churches, episcopal confirmation for orders outside the diocese, penalties for resisting episcopal decree, fines on idolaters split between Christ and the king.

b.bio: No surviving record identifies this author; the sources at hand describe other bearers of similar names — a sixth-century bishop Principius of Le Mans and unrelated bishops of the same see — and must be set aside as homonyms. What can be said rests on the work itself: a short Life of Hildebert, printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 171, which defends Bishop Hildebert of Le Mans against moral accusation. It argues that a pupil may reject his teacher's heresy, treats Hildebert as a monk of Cluny whose writings prove Benedictine monasticism, declares Ivo's accusatory letter spurious, and holds that unanimous election refutes charges of misconduct. Its citations of Baronius, Orderic Vitalis, Honorius II, Paschal II, Louis VI, and Henry I place its composition after the sixteenth century.
b.s: His single held work is a defense of Hildebert of Le Mans's reputation and episcopal election, written against partisans of Geoffrey the dean and Count Helias and against Baronius's account.

b.bio:
Proclus of Constantinople (c. 390 – 24 July 446) — Proclus was born around 390 and became a reader in Constantinople as a youth, studying rhetoric under private tutors. He served as personal secretary to Archbishop Atticus; Sisinius consecrated him bishop of Cyzicus, but Nestorian sympathizers in the city rejected him and he returned to Constantinople to preach. In 429 he preached before Nestorius in defense of calling Mary Theotokos. On Sisinius's death he was chosen archbishop of Constantinople, holding the see from 434 until his death on 24 July 446. A traditional link to John Chrysostom as disciple and ordainer is now considered a later medieval construction.

Dionysius Exiguus (c. 470 – c. 544) — Dionysius Exiguus ('the Humble') was a monk born in Scythia Minor (modern Romania) who lived in Rome from around 500 until his death before 544. Cassiodorus calls him a Scythian, learned in both Greek and Latin; later writers honor him as an abbot, though Cassiodorus describes him as still an ordinary monk late in life. He translated 401 church canons from Greek into Latin — the Apostolic Canons, Nicaea, Constantinople, Chalcedon, Sardica — and compiled the decretals of popes from Siricius to Anastasius II. His Collectiones canonum Dionysianae carried great authority in the West. At Pope John I's request he prepared in 525 the Easter reckoning that introduced Anno Domini dating. The works here include his canonical collections and Easter letters alongside his Latin translations: Gregory of Nyssa on the creation of man, the Life of Pachomius, and the finding of John the Baptist's head. A Synodal Letter is also held under his name, though some works long attributed to him (e.g. Cyril of Alexandria's synodical letter) are now assigned to Marius Mercator.
b.s: A leading pulpit orator of the Nestorian controversy whose sermons defended the title Theotokos, Mary's perpetual virginity, and the hypostatic union, making him one of the earliest formative Marian theologians; the works held here are his orations, homilies, and letters against Nestorius and Theodore of Mopsuestia.

b.bio:
Proclus Constantinopolitanus (c. 390 – 24 July 446) — Proclus was born around 390 and became a reader (lector) in Constantinople at a young age, studying rhetoric. He served as secretary to Patriarch Atticus, who ordained him deacon and priest. Under Sissinius he was appointed Archbishop of Cyzicus, but the Cyzicans chose a bishop of their own and he was not accepted there. Passed over for the patriarchate in favor of Nestorius in 428, he gained prominence by preaching in defense of the title Theotokos during the Nestorian controversy. After Nestorius's deposition at Ephesus (431), he was elected Archbishop of Constantinople in 434 and held the see until his death on 24 July 446.

Marius Mercator (c. 390–after 451) — Marius Mercator, probably born in Northern Africa about 390, died shortly after 451. In 417 or 418 he was in Rome, where he wrote two anti-Pelagian treatises and submitted them to Augustine of Hippo, who answered him in Epistula 193. From 429 to about 448 he lived in Constantinople. His writings are polemics against Pelagianism and Nestorianism and compilations of excerpts from Greek writers — Cyril of Alexandria, Nestorius, Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret — which preserved the documents of the Nestorian controversy in Latin.
b.s: A leading preacher of the Nestorian controversy and an early Marian theologian; the work held here is his interpretation of a prayer (PL 67).

b.bio: Prosper ex Manichaeo Catholicus (unknown) — The library prints this name as 'Prosper ex Manichaeo Catholicus' — a former Manichaean who converted to Catholicism and signed a public profession of faith with anathematisms against his former sect, placed by Migne in the sixth century (PL 65). He is not Prosper of Aquitaine (c. 390–c. 455), the Augustinian correspondent and chronicler whom the encyclopedias describe; that identification belongs to a different author and is set aside here.
b.s: His single short work here is a first-hand renunciation of Manichaeism: a series of anathematisms denying two principles, the divine substance trapped in matter, and the Manichaean Paraclete, paired with a creed affirming creation by the one good God, Christ's true flesh, and the resurrection of this flesh.

b.bio: Protadius (Prothadius, Prothade) succeeded Nicetas as bishop of Besançon around 613 and died there around 624 or 626; the two death dates come from different references. He stood close to King Chlothar II and was remembered for care for the poor. The vita printed under BHL 6974 is late and vague: Molinier calls it very posthumous, and the Histoire littéraire assigns it to the tenth century. A twelfth-century copy preserves liturgical prescriptions he gave his clergy.
b.s: The library holds a single liturgical text attributed to him: a Besançon pontifical surviving in Tours manuscripts, whose calendar predates its eleventh-century obits and which records that the bodies of Silvestre and Anian rest at the Saint-Agapit chapel, Anian counting among Besançon's bishop-confessors.

b.bio:
Proterius of Alexandria (d. 457) — Proterius was a presbyter and church-steward under Dioscorus of Alexandria and was left in charge of the see when Dioscorus went to Chalcedon. After the council deposed Dioscorus, Emperor Marcian ordered a new election, and Proterius was consecrated patriarch (sources date his enthronement to 451 or 452). Most Alexandrians remained loyal to Dioscorus; riots met Proterius throughout his tenure. In 457 the anti-Chalcedonian party elected Timothy Aelurus, and Proterius was killed — sources differ on whether a Coptic mob or the Byzantine garrison murdered him. He is commemorated as a hieromartyr on February 28. The letter held here defends the Alexandrian paschal reckoning: it upholds Theophilus's Easter cycle as binding, fixes Easter from passion chronology on the 17th moon, defers the feast when the full moon falls on Sunday as the fathers did, rejects Jewish passover reckoning, and condemns Sunday fasting as Manichaean.

Dionysius Exiguus (c. 470 – c. 544) — Dionysius Exiguus ('the Humble') was a monk born in Scythia Minor (modern Romania) who lived in Rome from around 500 until his death before 544. Cassiodorus calls him a Scythian, learned in both Greek and Latin; later writers honor him as an abbot, though Cassiodorus describes him as still an ordinary monk late in life. He translated 401 church canons from Greek into Latin — the Apostolic Canons, Nicaea, Constantinople, Chalcedon, Sardica — and compiled the decretals of popes from Siricius to Anastasius II. His Collectiones canonum Dionysianae carried great authority in the West. At Pope John I's request he prepared in 525 the Easter reckoning that introduced Anno Domini dating. The works here include his canonical collections and Easter letters alongside his Latin translations: Gregory of Nyssa on the creation of man, the Life of Pachomius, and the finding of John the Baptist's head. A Synodal Letter is also held under his name, though some works long attributed to him (e.g. Cyril of Alexandria's synodical letter) are now assigned to Marius Mercator.
b.s: His letter to Leo is evidence for mid-fifth-century Alexandrian paschal computation and its appeal to Theophilus's cycle and patristic precedent.

b.bio: An anonymous writer whose single surviving work is preserved under the name of Julian. the surviving records here concern other figures bearing similar names — a fourth-century forger writing as Ignatius of Antioch and texts falsely attributed to Pope Julius I — and do not describe this author; they are set aside. What is known comes from the work itself: an apologetic poem that defends certain christological propositions attributed to Julian as capable of orthodox interpretation, and argues that imperial power should compel Monothelites to submit to the apostolic see of Peter, whose judgment binds on earth as God's judgment.
b.s: The library holds one page of polemic verse from PL 96 defending Julian's Christology and asserting papal primacy against the Monothelites and Pope Benedict II.

b.bio:
Ptolemy, uncle of Peter the Deacon (unknown) — None of The surviving records describes this Ptolemy. They cover two different men named Peter the Deacon — one Pope Gregory the Great's companion and secretary (d. c. 605), the other the twelfth-century librarian of Montecassino (c. 1107–1159) — and neither identifies an uncle named Ptolemy or attributes letters to him. What can be said rests entirely on the library record: under this name the library holds a set of letters printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 173, the same volume that carries the Montecassino Peter's writings. No dates, offices, places, or biography for Ptolemy are attested here.

Gregory, uncle of Peter the Deacon (unknown) — The library prints this name as 'Gregory, uncle of Peter the Deacon.' The surviving records describe Peter the Deacon of Rome (d. c. 605), the Benedictine monk and companion/secretary of Pope Gregory I who appears in the Dialogues 4.57; none of them names a Gregory who was Peter's uncle or gives any dates, offices, or biographical facts for him. Other Gregories in the sources — Gregory of Tours and Gregory the Great — are different persons and do not fit this attribution. What can be said rests on the library record alone.
b.s: His letters survive only as items in PL 173 alongside the correspondence of Peter the Deacon of Montecassino, which is presumably why he is remembered as that Peter's uncle.

w: Description of the City of Rome

b.bio: The library's record and the Documenta Catholica Omnia index place under the name Publius Victor a single work, the Descriptio Urbis Romae, printed among Latin writers of the fourth-to-fifth centuries in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 18. No source supplies birthplace, office, or biography for this author. He should not be confused with Pope Victor I; nothing connects the two beyond the name.
b.s: His one surviving work here is a history concerning the city of Rome, transmitted alongside other Roman antiquarian texts such as those of Pomponius Laetus in later collections.

w: Poem on the Deeds of Witigowo

b.bio: Purchard (also Burchard) was a monk of Reichenau, apparently an oblate, and perhaps later provost; some identify him with the abbot of Sankt Emmeram (1030–37), but this is uncertain. Around 995/96 he composed the Gesta Witigowonis, a dialogue poem in leonine hexameters between the personified monastery (Augia) and the poet, praising Abbot Witigowo's decade of rule (985–97). The work survives incomplete in an autograph manuscript at Karlsruhe.
b.s: The library holds his single surviving work, a panegyric dialogue defending Witigowo's abbacy — its building works, jurisdiction, and need for a powerful protector-abbot — against the envious, and it stands as a witness to pre-reform Ottonian monastic culture.

b.bio: Pierre de La Ramée, printed as Petrus Ramus, was born at Cuts in Picardy to a farming family and educated at the Collège de Navarre in Paris, taking his master of arts in 1536. He taught at the Collège du Mans and the Collège de l'Ave Maria before holding a chair at the Collège de France, attacking scholastic Aristotelianism and separating dialectic from rhetoric. A convert to Protestantism, he was killed in Paris during the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre on 26 August 1572. Note: the library's single item under this name, an 'Admonition' in Migne's Patrologia Latina vol. 74, belongs among the Latin Fathers and cannot be by this sixteenth-century author; the attribution appears misfiled.
b.s: His logical and rhetorical textbooks shaped university curricula across Europe between roughly 1550 and 1650; however, the work actually shelved here is a patristic text that predates him and does not represent his writings.

b.bio: Romanus was born at Gallese near Civita Castellana, son of Constantine, and became cardinal priest of San Pietro in Vincoli in 867. He was elected pope in August 897 amid the factional violence following the Cadaver Synod of Stephen VI; under him Formosus' body was retrieved from the Tiber and buried. He granted the pallium to Vitalis of Grado and confirmed possessions to the Spanish sees of Elna and Gerona. He died or was deposed after about four months — 'he was made a monk', a phrase often denoting deposition.
b.s: The two pages held here are privilege letters asserting papal and apostolic authority over church property — the very acts (confirmations for Grado, Elna, Gerona) his brief pontificate is remembered for.

b.bio: Silverius was a subdeacon at Rome when the Ostrogothic king Theodahad secured his election as bishop of Rome (probably consecrated 8 June 536) after the death of Agapetus I. He was the son of Pope Hormisdas. In 537 the Byzantine general Belisarius deposed him — sources connect this to Empress Theodora's support for his successor Vigilius and for Monophysite interests — and he was exiled to Palmarola, where he died on 2 December 537. The letter held here is a polemic written from exile against Vigilius and Belisarius: it defends Agapetus's condemnation of Patriarch Anthimus, denies that false witnesses may be brought against bishops, and asserts that an exiled bishop retains his office.
b.s: His single surviving letter is a first-hand protest of a deposed pope against the usurpation by Vigilius and Belisarius, arguing that deposition by force does not extinguish episcopal authority.

b.bio: Simplicius was bishop of Rome from 25 February 468 until his death on 2 or 10 March 483. The Liber Pontificalis records him as the son of a citizen of Tivoli named Castinus; his birth date is unknown. His pontificate spanned the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476, when Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus, an event that left the church's administration at Rome largely undisturbed. In the East he defended the Council of Chalcedon against the Monophysites (Eutychians), protesting to the emperors Leo I and the usurper Basiliscus when Eutychian partisans seized the sees of Alexandria and Antioch under Peter Mongus and Timothy Aelurus.
b.s: The letters held here show him exercising the vicariate authority of the apostolic see in defense of Chalcedonian bishops, ruling on illicit ordinations by deposed bishops, and regulating church property and revenues.

b.bio: Sixtus III (Xystus), a Roman and son of a priest named Xystus, was prominent among the Roman clergy before his election as bishop of Rome on 31 July 432. He had corresponded with Augustine and was accused—probably falsely, per Weber and Butler—of early sympathy with Pelagius; as pope he refused Julian of Eclanum readmission to communion. His pontificate is marked by efforts to reconcile Cyril of Alexandria and John of Antioch after Ephesus, approval of the council's acts, defense of Roman claims over Illyricum against Proclus of Constantinople, and building at St. Mary Major and St. Lawrence-Without-the-Walls. He died in 440.
b.s: The letters held here are his conciliatory correspondence with the eastern bishops after the Nestorian controversy, including the letter to Acacius of Beroea answering eastern appeals for peace following Celestine.

b.bio: The library holds under this name a single epistle printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 55, a historical letter that cites Leo the Great and Eusebius and names Manichaeans, Priscillianists, Pelagians, and Eutychians as heretical parties. That content places the author in the fifth- or sixth-century Latin church. He should not be confused with Peter Thomas (c. 1305–1366), the French Carmelite friar and papal legate canonized in 1628: the surviving records here describe only that later Carmelite, whose works and century do not match the epistle held under this name.
b.s: His one work here is a historical epistle engaging the christological and anti-Pelagian controversies of its age through the authority of Leo the Great and Eusebius.

b.bio: Vitalian was bishop of Rome from his consecration on 30 July 657 until his death on 27 January 672. According to the Liber Pontificalis he was a native of Segni and son of Anastasius; his date of birth is unknown and nothing is known of his life before elevation to the Holy See. His pontificate sought conciliation with Emperor Constans II amid the Monothelite controversy and saw the secession of Ravenna from papal authority. The letters printed under his name in PL 87 concern appeals to the apostolic see, the restoration of an innocent condemned bishop, and disputes involving the monks of Fleury.
b.s: The letters here show seventh-century Roman claims that sentences contrary to the canons are void, that appeals to the apostolic see may not be refused, and that Peter's binding and loosing grounds Roman authority.

b.bio: Zosimus was bishop of Rome from 18 March 417 until his death on 26 December 418 (some sources give 27 December), succeeding Innocent I. The Liber Pontificalis calls him a Greek, son of Abram(ius); Harnack inferred Jewish origin from the father's name, but Duchesne rejected that inference. Nothing is recorded of his life before his election. His pontificate was consumed by jurisdictional disputes: he backed Patroclus of Arles as metropolitan and papal vicar over Gaul against Heros, intervened in Africa in the Pelagian affair involving Coelestius, and quarreled with his own clergy. He was succeeded by Boniface I.
b.s: The letters held here are the instruments of his Gaulish policy — metropolitan authority, appeals reserved to Rome for grave causes, and rulings touching Coelestius — and remain primary evidence for early fifth-century Roman claims to jurisdiction.

b.bio: Paride de Grassi, born in Bologna around 1470 into a family with roots in the law faculty at the University of Bologna and the College of Notaries, entered the papal Office of Ceremonies in May 1504 as a participating ceremonialist and rose to its presidency. Julius II made him bishop of Pesaro on 4 April 1513; he was consecrated that 16 May by Achille Cardinal Grassi and held the see until his death in Rome on 10 June 1528. His diary records ceremonial life at the papal court from 1504 to 1521.
b.s: The work here is a fragment of his diary defending the secrecy and immutability of Roman liturgical rites against their publication, arguing that only the pope may alter them.

b.bio: Pierre de Marca was born at Gan in Béarn on 24 January 1594 and died in Paris on 29 June 1662. Trained in law at the University of Toulouse, he served as councillor (1615) and president (1621) of the Parliament of Pau and as intendant of Béarn (1631), helping restore Catholicism there. After his wife's death in 1631 he devoted himself to scholarship on religious controversy, history, and canon law, publishing the Gallican treatise Concordia sacerdotii et imperii (1641). He entered the priesthood, became Bishop of Couserans in 1641, later Archbishop of Toulouse, and was installed as Archbishop of Paris on 5 June 1662, dying weeks later. He was a working historian as well as a prelate; Britannica credits him with apparently coining the French term le moyen âge in 1641.
b.s: The library holds a single page from Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 96) in which Marca, as a critical editor of Isidore, argues that the printed edition of Isidore is corrupt and that Isidore's chronicle is chronologically exact, against Roderic of Toledo.

b.bio: This is not a single author but a shelfmark: volume 2 of the Patrologia Graeca, J.-P. Migne's nineteenth-century collection of Greek patristic texts with facing Latin translations. The volume gathers pre-Nicene works under one cover: Clement of Rome, the Epistle of Barnabas, Hermas, the Epistle to Diognetus, and the anonymous Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs. The items held here are the volume's apparatus — addenda, analytical index, title page, and table of contents — not a treatise by one hand.
b.s: The works catalogued here are the volume's index and addenda; readers should consult them as a map to PG 2's pre-Nicene contents rather than as an author's argument.

w: A Critical Inquiry into the Integrity of the Received Text of the Epistles of St. Ignatius of Antioch

b.bio: This shelf gathers the contents of volume 5 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, not the work of one author. The volume prints Ignatius of Antioch, Polycarp, Melito of Sardis, Papias, Apollonius of Ephesus and other early writers, together with front matter by later editors: Isaac Vossius's preface, Jean-Baptiste Cotelier's judgment on the Ignatian epistles, and vindications of Ignatius. The library's held items from this volume are almost entirely that apparatus: dissertations, introductions, and a critical inquiry into the integrity of the received text of Ignatius's epistles.
b.s: The works here defend the authenticity of the longer Greek recension of Ignatius's letters against Jean Daillé's attack on it and against William Cureton's claim that the short Syriac recension preserves the original, while surveying what Ignatius teaches on the eucharist as Christ's suffering flesh, episcopal succession, and separation from the assembly.

w: Indices of Authors Cited by Justin, Tatian, Athenagoras, and Theophilus
Works of Justin Martyr, Tatian, Athenagoras, Theophilus of Antioch, and Hermias the Philosopher

b.bio: PG 6 is not a single author but volume 6 of Jacques Paul Migne's Patrologia Graeca, the 161-volume collection of Greek patristic texts published in Paris between 1857 and 1866. This volume gathers five second-century Greek apologists: Justin Martyr, Tatian, Athenagoras of Athens, Theophilus of Antioch, and Hermias the Philosopher. The library holds it as two records: the collected works themselves and indices of authors cited by Justin, Tatian, Athenagoras, and Theophilus. The volume also contains Migne's editorial apparatus — preface, elenchus, and discussions of Justin's manuscripts and translations.
b.s: A reader holding this volume has the standard printed Greek text (with facing Latin) of the major ante-Nicene Greek apologists, the base edition behind most later translations of these writers.

b.bio: Prudentius Maran, born at Sezanne in the Marne, entered the Benedictines at the abbey of St. Faron near Meaux on 30 January 1703 and studied at St. Denis. He worked at Saint-Germain-des-Prés on the edition of Cyril of Jerusalem begun by Antoine-Augustin Touttée. In 1734 Cardinal Bissy forced him to leave Saint-Germain-des-Prés, suspecting him of dissuading his confreres from accepting the Bull Unigenitus; after a year at Orbais and a stay at Saint-Martin de Pontoise, he moved in 1737 to Blancs-Manteaux, where he remained until his death in Paris in 1762. He was a patrologist whose critical editions of the Greek and Latin Fathers carried long introductions.
b.s: The work held here is his preface to the edition of Justin Martyr and the other Greek apologists (Justin, Tatian, Athenagoras, Theophilus, Hermias) that is his acknowledged masterpiece; it is preserved here in PG 6.

w: On the Doctrine of Saint Hippolytus

b.bio: This record covers Patrologia Graeca volume 10, not a single author. The volume gathers short early Christian writers: Alexander of Jerusalem (bishop and martyr), Anatolius of Laodicea in Syria, Pope Anterus, Archelaus of Mesopotamia, Asterius Urbanus, and Caius the presbyter. The largest item held here is a dissertation on Saint Hippolytus, which surveys the evidence for his identity and office, arguing that he was bishop of Portus rather than Rome, a Gaul by origin and disciple of Irenaeus, flourishing under Alexander Severus.
b.s: The works here are chiefly a citation-survey and polemic on the contested figure of Hippolytus, weighing Jerome, Eusebius, Photius, Tillemont, Fabricius, Scaliger, and Basnage against one another.

b.bio: This record is not a single author but Migne's Patrologia Graeca volume 18, one of the 161 volumes of Greek patristic and Byzantine texts published in Paris between 1857 and 1866 under Jacques Paul Migne's Imprimerie Catholique. The library holds only the volume's title page and tables of contents, so no individual writer or text from within it can be identified here.
b.s: The works held are the front matter of PG 18; readers seeking a specific author should consult that author's own entry rather than this anthology record.

w: Prefaces and Notes of Previous Editors

b.bio: PG 33 is not the work of one author but a Patrologia Graeca volume collecting several: Cyril of Jerusalem heads it, followed by Peter II and Timothy of Alexandria, Apollinarius of Laodicea, Isaac the Great, and Diodore of Tarsus. The pages this library holds are the volume's editorial apparatus — title page, table of contents, and the prefaces and notes of previous editors. Those editors' notes argue for manuscript collation as the basis of Cyril's catecheses' text, defend verbal fidelity in translation of sacred doctrine, and deploy patristic citation against modern innovators, including André Rivet.
b.s: The held pages are the scholarly front matter through which readers reach Cyril of Jerusalem's catechetical lectures; their polemical prefaces show how seventeenth- to nineteenth-century editors used the fathers against contemporary opponents such as Rivet.

b.bio: This entry is not a single author but Migne's Patrologia Graeca volume 38, which source:1 titles 'Gregorii Nazianzeni Theologi Opera Omnia' — the complete works of Gregory of Nazianzus. The Patrologia Graeca is an edited collection of Greek patristic writings in 161 volumes (bound as 166), published by J.-P. Migne's Imprimerie Catholique, Paris, 1857–1866; it includes the Cappadocian Fathers, among them Gregory of Nazianzus. The library's holdings under this name are the volume's front matter only: a title page, a table of contents, and 'The Analytic,' with no text pages. The theses mined from the volume's pages (Adam's fall as total, all humanity sinned in Adam, death passed from Adam to all, the active life joined with the contemplative, the weak to be healed not crushed) belong to Gregory's orations as printed there. No source in this record gives Gregory's dates, so none are asserted here.
b.s: The works held are the navigational front matter of PG 38, the Migne volume collecting Gregory of Nazianzus's complete works; readers should consult the volume itself for the orations these contents describe.

b.bio: This entry is not an author but a volume of Jacques Paul Migne's Patrologia Graeca, the 161-volume collection of Greek patristic and Byzantine texts published in Paris, 1857–1866. The library holds only the title page and table of contents of PG 39, with no works or pages under this heading, so no author can be identified from the record. Migne's series prints Greek text with a facing Latin translation and arranges volumes roughly chronologically.
b.s: The record identifies PG 39 as a Migne anthology volume rather than a named writer; readers should consult the volume's contents list to find which authors it collects.

b.bio: This entry is not a single author but volume 43 of Jacques-Paul Migne's Patrologia Graeca, the nineteenth-century Paris collection of Greek Christian writers with facing Latin translations. The library holds from it chiefly apparatus — addenda, an analytical index, title page, and table of contents — together with a short piece on Nonnus of Panopolis. The mined pages are liturgical-historical rather than patristic exegesis proper: they treat the lenten fast, communion of the presanctified gifts, Good Friday and Holy Saturday observance at Rome, Italo-Greek rite manuscripts, and unnotated chant, citing modern scholars such as Leo Allatius, Balsamon, Heinsius, Scaliger, Suidas, and Fabricius.
b.s: The volume matters here as a case study in how Migne's appendices and addenda carry early-modern liturgical scholarship — including polemic against Nicetas Pectoratus, Meursius, and Armenian tetradites — alongside the patristic texts they annotate.

b.bio: PG 65 is not the work of one author but a Migne anthology gathering several late-antique Greek ecclesiastical writers. The volume's index lists Severian of Gabala, Theophilus of Alexandria, Palladius, Philostorgius, Atticus of Constantinople, Proclus of Constantinople, Flavian, and three authors named Marcus: Marcus Eremita, Marcus Diadochus, and Marcus Diaconus. The library holds only the volume's title page and table of contents; no individual text from these authors is present in this record.
b.s: The works held here are front matter for Migne's Patrologia Graeca volume 65, useful chiefly as a guide to which late-fourth- and fifth-century Greek authors and texts that volume contains.

b.bio: This entry is not an author but a shelf mark: volume 66 of the Patrologia Graeca, the 161-volume collection of Greek patristic and Byzantine texts edited by Jacques Paul Migne in Paris between 1857 and 1866. Each volume gathers works by one or more Greek writers with facing Latin translations. the surviving records describe the series generally and do not state which authors or works fill volume 66, so no specific contents can be asserted beyond what the library record shows.
b.s: The works held under this name are only front-matter items — a title page and tables of contents; readers seeking the actual authors of PG 66 should consult the series' author index rather than this placeholder entry.

b.bio: This entry covers the appended matter in Migne's Patrologia Graeca volume 85 rather than a single patristic author; the volume's main text is Basil, bishop of Seleucia (per the volume's printed title 'Basilii Seleuciensis Episcopi Opera Omnia et Alii'). The four items held here are front and back matter: a title page, a table of contents, a Notice, and an Appendix to the Fifth Century. The Notice and Appendix are scholarly apparatus in the manner of Angelo Mai's Spicilegium Romanum, which they cite. They discuss palimpsest fragments associated with the Cryptensis/Grottaferrata codex, arguing that the fragments are not plagiarized from John Malalas, that Byzantine chroniclers did borrow from earlier historians, and that two misbound bifolia result from the rebinder's work, with Grottaferrata monks customarily reusing old parchment.
b.s: The works here are not theology but the editorial and philological case for dating and attributing the Cryptensis chronicle fragments printed at the end of PG 85, directed against identification with Malalas.

w: John the Faster, Patriarch of Constantinople

b.bio: John IV, called Nesteutes or 'the Faster,' was born in Constantinople to artisan parents and worked as a goldsmith before entering church service. Patriarch John III Scholasticus ordained him deacon at Hagia Sophia; he later served as sakellarios under Eutychius and was made patriarch by Emperor Tiberius II in 582. He mediated disputes between the Orthodox and Monophysites and assumed the contested title of ecumenical patriarch, provoking Roman objection. He died in Constantinople on 2 September 595.
b.s: The library holds his penitential canons, which treat repentance and remission of sins and argue that God wills not the sinner's death but repentance, against those who make penances too heavy.

b.bio: This entry is not an author but a printed volume: Patrologia Graeca 89, one of the 161 volumes of Greek patristic texts published by Jacques Paul Migne's Imprimerie Catholique in Paris between 1857 and 1866. Its full title is 'Anastasii Synaitae et Aliorum Opera Omnia' — works of Anastasius of Sinai together with miscellaneous shorter pieces by other Greek writers. The library holds only the volume's title page and table of contents, so no individual text from it can be attributed here.
b.s: The record holds only the front matter of PG 89; readers seeking the contents should consult the volume itself under Anastasius of Sinai or the individual authors Migne prints there.

b.bio: This entry is a volume of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, not a single author: PG 91 collects works printed under the name of Maximus the Confessor, whom Migne's index places in the seventh century. The library holds only the volume's title page and table of contents, so no text is present here. The contents as listed include material on Pseudo-Dionysius and Gregory of Nazianzus, difficulties concerning the saints, and a letter of Gregory the Great to Patriarch Germanus of Constantinople.
b.s: The record is a container for PG 91 rather than a work by one hand; readers should consult the table of contents to see which texts the volume assigns to Maximus and which to other authors such as Gregory the Great.

b.bio: PG 93 is not an author but volume 93 of Jacques-Paul Migne's Patrologia Graeca, the 161-volume Paris collection of Greek patristic texts published 1857–1866. Printed in 1865, this volume gathers works of Olympiodorus deacon of Alexandria, Hesychius of Jerusalem, Leontius of Neapolis in Cyprus, and Leontius of Damascus, each with Greek text and facing Latin translation. The library's holdings from this volume are front matter: the title page, table of contents, and the editorial notice on Hesychius of Jerusalem.
b.s: The notice printed here distinguishes presbyter Hesychius of Jerusalem, who died circa AD 433 and wrote the allegorical commentary on Leviticus that follows in the volume, from the bishop of the same name, and notes that an oration on Andrew was misattributed to Thomas by copyist error.

w: Analytical Indices (Subject Index, First/Second Index, Table of Contents)

b.bio: This shelf-mark is not a single author but Migne's Patrologia Graeca volume 96, which collects the works of John of Damascus together with those of John of Nicaea, John the Patriarch of Constantinople, and Joannes Euboeensis. The library's holdings under this name are the volume's analytical apparatus: subject and first/second indices and a table of contents spanning 29 pages. The mined content reflects the volume's range rather than one writer's program: passages on Christology against Timothy Aelurus and Acacius of Melitene, on the Filioque attributed to Spanish insertion and Roman adoption by its own authority, on latria versus douleia, eastward prayer as apostolic tradition, and on Adam's lack of comprehensive knowledge.
b.s: The works here are navigational indices to PG 96, whose principal author, John of Damascus, was the last of the Greek Fathers and the most authoritative theologian for the Eastern Church.

b.bio: This is not an author but a shelf mark: volume 97 of Jacques Paul Migne's Patrologia Graeca, the 161-volume collection of Greek patristic and Byzantine texts printed in Paris between 1857 and 1866. Volume 97 gathers works under three headings — Andrew of Crete, John Malalas, and Elias of Crete. The items held here are the volume's front matter for the Malalas section: prolegomena and prefaces discussing the chronicler's identity and date, indices, and tables of contents. The prolegomena argue against earlier scholars — Humphrey Hody, Edmund Chilmead, Gerhard Vossius, Leo Allatius — who had disputed whether 'Malalas' was a name or an epithet and when the chronicler wrote.
b.s: A reader holding these pages has the editorial apparatus of Migne's Malalas, not a patristic text; its value is as a guide to the older scholarship on the Chronicle before modern critical editions.

b.bio: This entry is not a single author but Migne's Patrologia Graeca volume 98, an anthology first published in Paris in 1865. The volume gathers works attributed to Germanus I, Patriarch of Constantinople, together with texts under the names of Cosmas of Jerusalem, Gregory II, Tarasius, Patriarch of Constantinople, and several minor figures including deacons and monks of Constantinople. The library's holding consists only of the volume's title page and table of contents; the individual treatises themselves are not held here.
b.s: As a shelf entry this record points readers to the Migne printing of Germanus of Constantinople's dogmatic letters, orations, and related eighth- to ninth-century Greek texts, rather than to any one work.

w: Appendices to the Chronology of Eutychius
Glossary of Terms in Theophanes and Leo Grammaticus
Index of Memorable Subjects and Terms
Index of Notable Matters Found in the Syntagma
Indexes to the Annals of Eutychius

b.bio: The name as printed here is a volume label, not a single author: Migne's PG 104 collects works of Photius of Constantinople, Petrus Siculus, Peter bishop of Argos, and Bartholomew of Edessa. Photius, twice patriarch of Constantinople in the ninth century, dominates the volume; his Bibliotheca and Amphilochia are excerpted here. The library's holdings under this heading are paratextual: an index of memorable subjects and terms (32 pages), plus title page, refutation notice, index to the Syntagma, and table of contents. The sources give no exact birth or death years for any of the four men, so no precise dates are asserted.
b.s: This entry is a navigational apparatus for Migne's PG 104 rather than a work by one author; its value is as a finding aid to Photius's Bibliotheca and related texts in that volume.

w: Additions to Euthymius; Index of the Alexiad
Testimonies of Illustrious Men Concerning the Menologium of Emperor Basil

b.bio: This entry is a shelf label for volume 117 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, not a single author. The five items held are the front matter of an early modern printed edition of the Menologium attributed to Emperor Basil II: a dedication to Pope Benedict XIII, a survey of testimonies by learned men concerning that menologium, and printer's preliminaries. The dedication and testimonies argue that the menologium was commissioned by Basil Porphyrogennetos before 984, that it equals the Latin martyrologies and kalendaria, and that multiple divergent Greek menologia circulated; they engage Baronius, Leo Allatius, and Ughelli. No personal author can be named from these records.
b.s: The works here are the editorial apparatus defending the authenticity and authority of the Menologion of Basil II against Baronius's doubts.

w: Analytical Index to the Logical Epitome of Nicephorus Blemmida
Catalogue of the Books of the Monastery on the Island of Patmos
Ephraim the Chronographer, Theoleptus Metropolitan of Philadelphia, and George Pachymeres: Title Page
Index to the Byzantine History of Nicephorus Gregoras
Index to the History of Pachymeres

b.bio: This entry covers the anonymous material gathered in volume 149 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, a volume whose principal named contents are the Byzantine History of Nikephoros Gregoras. The library's holdings under this heading are not treatises by a single writer but apparatus and minor documents: tables of contents, an index of Greek vocabulary, an index to Gregoras' history, and a two-page catalogue of the books of the Monastery of St John on Patmos. The citation-survey page lists Basil, John Chrysostom, Theodoret, Leo Magister, Matthew Cantacuzenus, Victor priest of Antioch, Titus of Bostra, and Macarius of Philadelphia. No dates or identity can be asserted for these unnamed compilers.
b.s: The works here are finding-aids and a monastic book-catalogue attached to PG 149; they matter to readers as pointers into Gregoras' history and as evidence for the holdings of the Patmos monastery.

b.bio: This shelf gathers material printed under Migne's Patrologia Graeca volume 158, which collects several minor Byzantine writers — Michael Clyca, Joannes Diaconus Adrianopolitanus, Esaias Cyprius, Hilario Monachus, Joannes Argyropulus, Josephus Cpolitanus Patriarcha, Job Monachus, Bartholomaeus de Jano Ord. Minorum, Nicolaus Barbarus Patricius Venetus, and anonymous authors. No single biography fits, since no source here gives dates or careers for any of them. What the record shows is a body of Greek Christian writing directed against Islam: it asserts that Muhammad learned his doctrine from heretical monks and from Jews and Nestorians, that his prophethood was staged deception, that Islamic practice derives from Jewish custom, and that the conquests were punishment for Christian sins.
b.s: The works held here are chiefly a long anonymous Register of anti-Islamic polemic plus the volume's scholarly apparatus (dissertation, lists, indexes), preserving how Byzantine writers explained Islam as a fabrication of heretics rather than as an independent religion.

w: Three Books of Observations on Pachymeres by Petrus Possinus

b.bio: Pierre Poussines (Petrus Possinus), a French Jesuit born in 1609 at Laurac in the diocese of Narbonne, entered the Society of Jesus at Toulouse in 1624 and taught humanities, rhetoric, and theology there and at Montpellier. Called to Rome in 1664 to continue Sacchini's history of the Society, he later held the chair of exegetical theology at the Roman College. He knew Greek well and studied the Fathers carefully, producing editions and translations of Greek authors, including Anna Comnena, a catena of the Greek Fathers on St Mark (Rome, 1673), Francis Xavier's letters, and the Specimen Sapientiae Indorum Veterum (1666). He died in 1686.
b.s: The work held here is his philological commentary on George Pachymeres, where he defends Latin doctrine — especially the Filioque and the Church's authority — against Pachymeres, Cantacuzenus, Abulpharagius, and the schismatics, while also settling points of Byzantine vocabulary such as allagion.

b.bio: Philotheos Kokkinos was born in Thessalonica around 1300 and died in Constantinople in 1379. A monk and later abbot of the Great Laura on Mount Athos, he was an advocate of Hesychasm and a close friend of Gregory Palamas. He served twice as Ecumenical Patriarch: appointed by John VI Kantakouzenos in August 1353, deposed by John V Palaiologos in December 1354, and restored on 8 October 1364 until August 1376. He opposed Emperor John V's plans for political reunion with the popes Urban V and Gregory XI, favoring instead an authentic union-council to resolve differences with the Western Church. The Orthodox Church commemorates him on 11 October as a 'Protector of Orthodoxy.'
b.s: The work held here presents his doctrinal teaching on the Trinity, the incarnation, and Christ's atoning death, arguing against Arius, the Eunomians, and Nicephorus Gregoras.

b.bio: This entry is not a single author but a volume of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, numbered 86 in that series. The library's holdings under this name are the volume's front matter and analytical indices rather than a complete text. The indices point to material treating sin as a voluntary act of the will, the division of sins into bodily and spiritual kinds, and charity and fasting as remedies that restore vision of God.
b.s: The works here are the analytical apparatus of PG 86, useful for locating discussions of sin, virtue, and the remedies of charity and fasting within the volume.

w: On the Destruction of the City of Jerusalem
Summary of the History of the Destruction of the City of Jerusalem

b.bio: Pseudo-Hegesippus is the name scholars give to the anonymous author of a fourth-century Latin adaptation of Josephus' Jewish War in five books, On the Destruction of Jerusalem (De excidio Hierosolymitano). The manuscripts call the author Hegesippus, a corruption of the name Josephus; he is not the second-century Greek chronicler Hegesippus. Migne prints the work among the writings of Ambrose of Milan (Patrologia Latina 15). The ascription to Ambrose is old but disputed, and the author is usually treated as unknown.
b.s: A Christian retelling of the Jewish War that reads the fall of Jerusalem as divine judgment on the Jews for rejecting Christ; widely read in the Latin West.

b.bio: Letters forged under Pope Damasus's name: the exchange with Jerome prefacing the Liber pontificalis and the Pseudo-Isidorian letters.

Camillo Borghese, born at Rome on 17 September 1550 (Britannica gives 17 September 1552), trained in jurisprudence at Perugia and Padua and became a canonist of standing. Clement VIII made him cardinal in 1596 and Cardinal-Vicar of Rome; he was elected pope on 16 May 1605 after the death of Leo XI and died 28 January 1621. He ruled from the decretals rather than diplomacy, defending ecclesiastical jurisdiction — against Venice by interdict in 1606, and in 1616 instructing Bellarmine to warn Galileo against teaching Copernicanism as fact. His printing privilege granted exclusive publication rights and required an imprimatur from the Master of the Sacred Palace.
b.s: The work here shows the early modern papacy treating printing control — privilege, imprimatur, and spiritual penalty — as an instrument of church governance.
